knowledge_statements.title: Integral Maximum Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integrality theorem for finite directed maximum-flow instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with distinct vertices \(s,t\) and integer capacities \(u_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(a\in A\). Then the maximum-flow problem admits an optimal flow \(f\) satisfying \(f_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every arc. In particular, Ford–Fulkerson initialized at the zero flow and augmented along residual \(s\)-\(t\) paths preserves integrality and terminates at an integral maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite network with nonnegative integer capacities has an integer-valued maximum flow; integral augmentations preserve this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a maximum flow \(f\) with \(f_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-Max Formula for a Minimum-Cost s-t Flow of Prescribed Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential duality for capacitated flows of fixed value, including primal and dual integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D=(V,A)$ have capacities $g:A\to\mathbb R_+$ and costs $c:A\to\mathbb R$, and suppose an $s$-$t$ flow of value $k$ exists. With $c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u)$, the minimum cost of such flows equals
$\max_\pi\left\{k\pi(t)+\sum_{uv\in A:\,c_\pi(uv)<0}c_\pi(uv)g(uv)\right\},$
where $\pi:V\to\mathbb R$, $\pi(s)=0$, and $0\le\pi(v)\le\pi(t)$ for every $v\in V$. If $g$ is integer-valued, an optimal flow may be chosen integral; if $c$ is integer-valued, an optimal $\pi$ may be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible prescribed flow value k, the minimum s-t flow cost equals a maximum over normalized vertex potentials of k times the sink potential plus the capacity-weighted negative reduced costs. Integral capacities give an integral optimal flow, and integral costs give an integral optimal potential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{cx:x\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of value }k\}=\max_\pi\left\{k\pi(t)+\sum_{c_\pi(uv)<0}c_\pi(uv)g(uv)\right\};\quad g\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow x^*\in\mathbb Z^A,\quad c\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow\pi^*\in\mathbb Z^V\text{ may be chosen}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical residual-path algorithm for static maximum flow, including finite optimum and unboundedness termination cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from any feasible flow \(x\), repeatedly choose an \(r\)-to-\(s\) augmenting path \(P\) in the residual digraph and augment by its residual width \(\varepsilon=\min\{\min_{e\in P^+}(u_e-x_e),\min_{e\in P^-}x_e\}\). If \(\varepsilon=\infty\), the maximum-flow value is unbounded. If no augmenting path exists, \(x\) is maximum and the vertices residually reachable from \(r\) determine a minimum cut. An augmenting path can be found in \(O(m)\) time. With integral capacities and an integral initial flow, every flow remains integral and every augmentation has value at least \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with any feasible flow and repeatedly augment by the bottleneck residual capacity of an r-to-s residual path. An infinite-width path certifies that no finite maximum exists; absence of an augmenting path certifies maximum flow, and the residually reachable vertices define a minimum cut. Each path search takes O(m) time. Integral capacities preserve integrality and make every augmentation at least one unit.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a directed network with source }r\text{, sink }s\text{, capacities }u,\text{ and }m=|E|.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon=\infty\Rightarrow\sup\operatorname{val}(x)=\infty;\qquad \text{no residual }r\text{-}s\text{ path}\Rightarrow x\text{ is maximum and }\delta(R)\text{ is a minimum cut}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential duality for capacitated minimum-cost flows of prescribed value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General integer-capacity extension of the unit-capacity k-braid theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let D=(V,A), g:A\to\mathbb Z_+, c:A\to\mathbb R_+, and suppose a feasible s-t flow of value k exists. For a potential \pi, let c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u). Then
\[
\min\{cz:z\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of value }k\}
=
\max_\pi\left\{k\pi(t)+\sum_{uv\in A:\,c_\pi(uv)<0}c_\pi(uv)g(uv)\right\}.
\]
A feasible value-k flow z is minimum-cost if and only if some potential \pi satisfies, for every uv\in A,
\[
c_\pi(uv)>0\Rightarrow z(uv)=0,\qquad c_\pi(uv)<0\Rightarrow z(uv)=g(uv).
\]
If c is integer-valued, an optimal potential may be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative costs and nonnegative integer capacities, the minimum cost of a feasible source-to-sink flow of prescribed value k equals a maximum over node potentials. A feasible flow is optimal exactly when positive-reduced-cost arcs carry zero flow and negative-reduced-cost arcs are saturated. Integer costs admit an integer optimal potential.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph with distinguished }s,t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{z:\,0\le z\le g,\,\operatorname{val}(z)=k}cz=\max_\pi\left(k\pi(t)+\sum_{c_\pi(e)<0}c_\pi(e)g(e)\right),\quad z\text{ is optimal}\iff\exists\pi\text{ satisfying the reduced-cost conditions};\ c\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow\pi\text{ may be integral}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly the requested amount \(c\) is dispatched through successive arcs, with every fully exhausted arc skipped in future calls; \(c=0\) leaves the state unchanged.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ and $s,t\in V$, an $s$-$t$ flow is a function $f:A\to\mathbb R$ such that $f(a)\ge 0$ for all $a\in A$ and $f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v))=f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))$ for every $v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}$. Its value is $f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(s))-f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(s))$, equivalently the net flow entering $t$. Given $c:A\to\mathbb R_+$, the flow is subject to $c$ when $f(a)\le c(a)$ for every $a$, and a maximum flow is a feasible flow of maximum value. A maximum flow exists; if $c$ is rational-valued, a rational-valued maximum flow exists. For any $f:A\to\mathbb R$ and $U\subseteq V$, $\operatorname{excess}_f(U):=f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))-f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U))$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s–t flow is a nonnegative arc function satisfying conservation at every vertex other than the source and sink. Its value is the net flow leaving the source, equivalently entering the sink. Capacity feasibility means that every arc flow is at most its capacity, and a maximum flow maximizes the value. A maximum exists, and rational capacities admit a rational maximum flow. The excess of a vertex set is its incoming flow minus its outgoing flow.
assumptions_latex: c:A\to\mathbb R_+\text{ for the capacitated problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{value}(f)=f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(s))-f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(s)),\qquad \operatorname{excess}_f(U)=f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))-f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U)).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition and converse construction for finite directed source-to-sink flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph, let \(s,t\in V\), and let \(f:A\to\mathbb R_{+}\) be an \(s\)-\(t\) flow. Then \(f\) is a nonnegative linear combination of at most \(|A|\) incidence vectors \(\chi^{P}\), where each \(P\) is a directed \(s\)-\(t\) path or a directed circuit. If \(f\) is integral, the coefficients may be chosen integral. Conversely, for directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\), the vector \(f=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\chi^{A(P_i)}\) is an integral \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative source-to-sink flow decomposes into at most the number of arcs many directed source-to-sink paths and directed circuits; an integral flow admits integral coefficients. Conversely, summing the arc-incidence vectors of k source-to-sink paths produces an integral flow of value k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\chi^{P_i},\quad r\le |A|,\quad \lambda_i\ge0;\qquad f\in\mathbb Z^{A}\Rightarrow \lambda_i\in\mathbb Z_{+}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum m-excess equals maximum subset deficit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-digraph min–max theorem with an integrality conclusion and identification of the algorithmic primal and dual optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) and \(g:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(f\le g\), and let \(m:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\widetilde m(V)=0\). Then
\[
\min_{f\le x\le g}\sum_{v\in V}(\Psi_x(v)-m(v))^+
=
\max_{X\subseteq V}(\varrho_f(X)-\delta_g(X)-\widetilde m(X))^+.
\]
If \(f,g,m\) are integral, an optimal feasible vector may be chosen integral. Moreover, Variant A returns a minimum-excess feasible vector \(x^*\) and a maximum-deficit set \(Z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a directed graph with compatible lower and upper arc bounds and vertex requirements summing to zero, the least possible total positive vertex excess of a bound-feasible vector equals the largest deficit of a vertex subset. Integral data admit an integral optimal vector, and Variant A returns both a primal and a deficit-set optimum.
assumptions_latex: f:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\},\quad g:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\},\quad f\le g.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{f\le x\le g}\operatorname{exc}_m(x)=\max_{X\subseteq V}\operatorname{def}(X),\quad (f,g,m\text{ integral})\Rightarrow(\exists\text{ integral optimal }x).

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Capacity Path Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed edge-disjoint path form of max-flow min-cut for unit capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with distinct vertices \(s,t\), and assign capacity \(u_a=1\) to every arc. The maximum number of pairwise arc-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum cardinality of an arc set whose deletion destroys every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path. Equivalently, an integral maximum flow decomposes into that many arc-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) path flows plus directed cycle flows; deleting the cycles leaves an optimal path packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a unit-capacity digraph, the largest arc-disjoint source-sink path packing equals the smallest source-sink arc cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph with \(s\ne t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\text{arc-disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}\}=\min\{|F|:G-F\text{ has no }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\).

notation.meaning: An arc set separating s from t.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational scaling preserves an exact discrete integrality structure but not unscaled integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every capacity of a finite \(s\)-\(t\) network is a nonnegative rational number. Choose an integer \(D>0\) such that \(D u_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for all arcs. The scaled network has an integral maximum flow \(g\); therefore \(f=g/D\) is a maximum flow of the original network and satisfies \(f_a\in D^{-1}\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Thus a rational maximum flow exists, although an integer-valued maximum flow need not exist in the original units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational capacities can be scaled to integers, yielding a rational maximum flow whose denominator divides a common capacity denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a common denominator \(D\), some maximum flow satisfies \(f_a\in D^{-1}\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every arc.

notation.meaning: A common positive denominator of all capacities.
Integral maximum flow in the scaled network.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Real-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates max-flow existence and duality from integrality and augmenting-path termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite and let \(u:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be arbitrary. The feasible-flow set is a nonempty compact polytope, so the flow-value functional attains a maximum. Max-flow min-cut duality remains valid: the maximum flow value equals the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. However, neither integer nor rational coordinates are guaranteed, and unrestricted Ford–Fulkerson augmenting-path choices are not guaranteed to terminate when capacities include irrational numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With arbitrary nonnegative real capacities, maximum flows and min-cut duality still exist, but arithmetic integrality and Ford–Fulkerson termination may fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f |f|=\min_{s\in S,\,t\notin S}u(\delta^+(S))\), with no general integrality or unrestricted termination guarantee.

notation.meaning: Total capacity leaving the cut source side S.

children.title: Integrality Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies integer capacities as sufficient and nonintegral capacities as an immediate obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integral maximum-flow conclusion does not extend to general nonintegral capacities. Consider the network with vertices \(s,t\) and one arc \(a=st\) of capacity \(u_a=1/2\). Its unique maximum flow has \(f_a=1/2\), so no integer-valued maximum flow exists. More generally, integral capacities guarantee an integral optimum, whereas rational capacities guarantee only an optimum on the lattice determined by a common denominator; arbitrary real capacities provide no rationality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single source-sink arc of capacity one-half already shows that nonintegral capacities need not admit an integral maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: The flow is measured in the original, unscaled capacity units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u_{st}=1/2\), every maximum flow satisfies \(f_{st}=1/2\notin\mathbb Z\).

notation.meaning: The sole directed arc from source to sink.

children.title: Termination Boundary
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic termination issues arising beyond discrete capacity regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the arithmetic boundary for unrestricted Ford–Fulkerson augmenting-path termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite network with rational capacities, choose a common denominator \(D\). Ford–Fulkerson started at zero and using any residual augmenting path increases the flow value by a positive multiple of \(1/D\); because the value is bounded above, only finitely many augmentations occur. This argument fails for irrational capacities: there exist finite networks with irrational capacities and sequences of augmenting-path choices producing infinitely many augmentations, possibly converging to a value strictly below the maximum. Thus unrestricted Ford–Fulkerson has a rational-capacity termination guarantee but no arbitrary-real-capacity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ford–Fulkerson always terminates for rational capacities, but suitable irrational instances and path choices can cause infinite, even suboptimal, augmentation sequences.
assumptions_latex: Ford–Fulkerson begins with the zero flow and permits arbitrary augmenting-path choices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\mathbb Q_{ge0}^{A}\) guarantees finite termination; \(u\in\mathbb R_{ge0}^{A}\) does not.

notation.meaning: A common denominator of all rational capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bounded Circulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed networks with nonnegative arc capacities and zero vertex balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(u:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). An upper-bounded circulation is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \[0\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=0\quad(v\in V).\] Thus every vertex has equal total inflow and outflow, while each arc carries a nonnegative amount no greater than its capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-bounded circulation respects every nonnegative arc capacity and conserves flow at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is feasible exactly when \(0\le f\le u\) and its balance is zero at every vertex.

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering vertex v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut Criterion for a Prescribed-Value s-t Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes existence of a feasible capacitated s-t flow of value k and records the integral-capacity consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ have capacity function $g$, let $s,t\in V$, and let $k\in\mathbb{R}$. A feasible $s$-$t$ flow of value $k$ exists if and only if $\delta_g(S)\ge k$ for every $S\subseteq V$ with $s\in S$ and $t\notin S$. If $g$ is integer-valued and such a flow exists, one may choose it integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible s-t flow of prescribed value k exists exactly when every cut whose source side contains s but not t has capacity at least k. With integral capacities, an integral such flow can be chosen.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph with capacity function }g
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists\text{ feasible $s$-$t$ flow of value }k\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall S\subseteq V:\ s\in S,\ t\notin S\Rightarrow\delta_g(S)\ge k\bigr),\quad g\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\Rightarrow\text{an integral flow may be chosen}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circulation Recovery and Cut Violation in the Auxiliary Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records both directions of the certificate interface in the auxiliary maximum-flow construction for bounded circulation feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the auxiliary-network construction with original arc lower bounds $f$, auxiliary digraph $D'$, auxiliary capacities $g'$, and target flow value $M$: (A) if $x'$ is a $g'$-feasible $s$-$t$ flow in $D'$ of value $M$, then the restriction $x=(f+x')|_A$ is a feasible circulation in the original digraph $D$; (B) if $\delta_{g'}(X\cup\{s\})<M$ for some $X\subseteq V$, then $X$ violates the corresponding circulation-feasibility cut inequality for $m\equiv0$.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise minimum-flow conditions in a two-sided bounded circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with lower-bound vector \(\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), a flow vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfies the lower-bound requirements precisely when \[f_a\ge \ell_a\qquad\text{for every }a\in A.\] In a two-sided bounded circulation these inequalities are imposed simultaneously with flow conservation and the upper inequalities \(f_a\le u_a\). A necessary condition for an arcwise feasible interval is \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every arc must carry at least its prescribed lower amount; each lower bound must not exceed the corresponding upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower-bound predicate is \(f_a\ge\ell_a\) for all \(a\in A\).

children.title: Feasible-Interval Interaction

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Interval Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-slack representation of simultaneous lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Write \(f=\ell+x\). Then the simultaneous arc conditions \(\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\) are equivalent to \[0\le x_a\le u_a-\ell_a\qquad(a\in A).\] If \(\partial z(v)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}z_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}z_a\), then the balance equation \(\partial f=b\) is equivalent to \[\partial x=b-\partial\ell.\] Thus lower bounds consume capacity and shift vertex balances; nonempty arc intervals alone do not guarantee a globally feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting lower bounds leaves residual capacities and shifts vertex balances; conservation still couples otherwise nonempty arc intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\le f\le u\) and \(\partial f=b\) if and only if \(f=\ell+x\), \(0\le x\le u-\ell\), and \(\partial x=b-\partial\ell\).

notation.meaning: flow remaining after mandatory lower-bound flow
vertexwise outflow minus inflow of arc vector z

knowledge_statements.title: Supply-Demand Transshipments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated transshipment with positive balances interpreted as supplies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). A feasible supply-demand transshipment is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) such that \[\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=b_v\quad(v\in V).\] Under this convention, \(b_v>0\) denotes supply and \(b_v<0\) denotes demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment routes flow within arc bounds so each vertex realizes its prescribed supply or demand balance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility means \(\ell\le f\le u\) and \(\partial f=b\).

notation.meaning: net supply at vertex v under the outflow-minus-inflow convention

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-flow complexity bound for bounded interval-balance transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic bound for finding a transshipment with two-sided arc bounds and vertex-balance intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If maximum flow on an \(n\)-vertex, \(m\)-arc network can be found in time \(\operatorname{MF}(n,m)\), then, given \(a,b,d,c\), a \(z\)-transshipment \(f\) satisfying \(d\le f\le c\) and \(a\le z\le b\) can be found in time \(O(\operatorname{MF}(n,m))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment respecting two-sided arc bounds and balance intervals can be found within asymptotically the runtime of maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: \text{Maximum flow can be found in time }\operatorname{MF}(n,m)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{bounded\ interval\ transshipment}}(n,m)=O(\operatorname{MF}(n,m)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral rounding of a fixed-value s-t flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves both the integer flow value and the componentwise floor-ceiling bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A) be a digraph, let s,t\in V, and let f be an s-t flow of value k\in\mathbb{Z}. Then there exists an integer s-t flow f' of value k such that \lfloor f(a)\rfloor\le f'(a)\le\lceil f(a)\rceil for every a\in A.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s-t flow having integer total value can be rounded arc by arc to an integer s-t flow of the same value, with every rounded arc value between the original value's floor and ceiling.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of value }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f'\in\mathbb{Z}^A:\ f'\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of value }k,\quad (\forall a\in A)\ \lfloor f(a)\rfloor\le f'(a)\le\lceil f(a)\rceil

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Criterion for an Uncapacitated Nonnegative b-Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-set characterization of nonnegative prescribed-excess transshipment feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph and let \(b:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(b(V)=0\). There exists a \(b\)-transshipment \(f\ge0\) if and only if \[b(U)\le0\] for every \(U\subseteq V\) with \(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative uncapacitated b-transshipment exists exactly when every vertex subset with no entering arcs has nonpositive prescribed total excess.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f\ge0:\operatorname{excess}_f=b\iff \forall U\subseteq V\text{ with }\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U)=\varnothing,\ b(U)\le0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gale Cut Criterion for Capacitated b-Transshipments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-capacitated nonnegative transshipment feasibility and integral feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph, \(c:A\to\mathbb R\), and \(b:V\to\mathbb R\) with \(b(V)=0\). There exists a \(b\)-transshipment \(f\) satisfying \(0\le f\le c\) if and only if \[c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge b(U)\] for every \(U\subseteq V\). If \(b\) and \(c\) are integer-valued, \(f\) may be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative b-transshipment within the arc capacities exists exactly when the capacity entering every vertex subset is at least that subset's prescribed total excess. Integral balances and capacities admit an integral transshipment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f:\operatorname{excess}_f=b,\ 0\le f\le c\iff \forall U\subseteq V,\ c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge b(U);\quad b,c\text{ integral}\Rightarrow f\text{ may be integral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut characterization for capacitated interval-balanced transshipments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative-flow specialization with upper arc capacities, balance intervals, and an integrality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(c:A\to\mathbb R_+\), and let \(a,b:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(a\le b\). There exist \(z\) and a \(z\)-transshipment \(f\) with \(0\le f\le c\) and \(a\le z\le b\) if and only if, for every \(U\subseteq V\), \[c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge \max\{a(U),-b(V\setminus U)\}.\] If \(a,b,c\) are integer-valued, \(f\) may be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative capacitated transshipment with balances in a prescribed interval exists exactly when every vertex subset satisfies the stated incoming-capacity inequality. Integral data admit an integral transshipment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z,f:\ f\text{ is a }z\text{-transshipment},\ 0\le f\le c,\ a\le z\le b\iff\forall U\subseteq V,\ c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge\max\{a(U),-b(V\setminus U)\};\quad a,b,c\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow f\in\mathbb Z^A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut characterization for interval-balanced bounded transshipments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility and integrality of a transshipment with two-sided arc bounds and vertex-balance intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(d,c:A\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(d\le c\), and let \(a,b:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(a\le b\). There exist \(z:V\to\mathbb R\) and a \(z\)-transshipment \(f\) such that \(d\le f\le c\) and \(a\le z\le b\) if and only if, for every \(U\subseteq V\), \[c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))-d(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U))\ge \max\{a(U),-b(V\setminus U)\}.\] If \(a,b,c,d\) are integer-valued, \(f\) may be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment respecting two-sided arc bounds and vertex-balance intervals exists exactly when the stated cut inequality holds for every vertex subset. With integral bounds, an integral transshipment exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z,f:\ f\text{ is a }z\text{-transshipment},\ d\le f\le c,\ a\le z\le b\iff \forall U\subseteq V,\ c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))-d(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U))\ge\max\{a(U),-b(V\setminus U)\};\quad a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow f\in\mathbb Z^A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut Criterion for a Two-Sided Bounded b-Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility characterization and integrality for prescribed-excess transshipments with lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph, let \(d,c:A\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(d\le c\), and let \(b:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(b(V)=0\). There exists a \(b\)-transshipment \(f\) with \(d\le f\le c\) if and only if \[c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))-d(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U))\ge b(U)\] for every \(U\subseteq V\). If \(b,d,c\) are integer-valued, \(f\) may be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prescribed-excess transshipment satisfying lower and upper arc bounds exists exactly when every vertex subset receives enough possible net inflow to meet its prescribed total excess. Integral data admit an integral feasible transshipment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f:\operatorname{excess}_f=b,\ d\le f\le c\iff \forall U\subseteq V,\ c(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))-d(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U))\ge b(U);\quad b,d,c\text{ integral}\Rightarrow f\text{ may be integral}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between simultaneous lower-and-upper balance feasibility and separate one-sided feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(d,c:A\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(d\le c\), and let \(a,b:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(a\le b\). A bounded \(z\)-transshipment \(f\) exists for some \(z\) with \(a\le z\le b\) if and only if there exist bounded transshipments \(f'\) and \(f''\), each satisfying \(d\le f',f''\le c\), whose respective balance vectors satisfy \(z'\ge a\) and \(z''\le b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment whose balance lies between prescribed lower and upper vectors exists exactly when the lower-balance and upper-balance requirements are separately feasible under the same arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists(f,z):d\le f\le c,\ a\le z\le b\bigr)\iff\bigl(\exists(f',z'):d\le f'\le c,\ z'\ge a\bigr)\land\bigl(\exists(f'',z''):d\le f''\le c,\ z''\le b\bigr).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Excess Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-bounded flows whose vertex excesses lie in prescribed intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, with arc bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and vertex excess bounds \(p,q\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). A bounded-excess flow is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \[\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad p_v\le \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a\le q_v\quad(v\in V).\] Necessarily \(\ell\le u\), \(p\le q\), and the realized excesses sum to zero because every arc contributes once positively and once negatively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-excess flow obeys arc intervals while allowing each vertex balance to vary within its own prescribed interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{f:\ell\le f\le u,\ p\le\partial f\le q\}\).

notation.meaning: outflow minus inflow at vertex v
permitted excess interval at vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine reduction from two-sided bounds to zero lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given arc bounds \(\ell\le f\le u\) and vertex balances \(\partial f=b\), set \(x_a=f_a-\ell_a\) and \(c_a=u_a-\ell_a\). Then \[0\le x_a\le c_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \partial x(v)=b_v-\partial\ell(v)\quad(v\in V).\] Conversely, every \(x\) satisfying these residual constraints yields a feasible original flow by \(f=x+\ell\). Hence the transformation is a bijection between the original feasible flows and the residual zero-lower-bound flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract every lower bound, reduce each capacity accordingly, and shift each vertex balance by the lower-bound vector's imbalance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\mapsto x=f-\ell\) bijects \(\{f:\ell\le f\le u,\partial f=b\}\) with \(\{x:0\le x\le u-\ell,\partial x=b-\partial\ell\}\).

notation.meaning: residual flow after subtracting lower bounds

children.title: Auxiliary Source Construction
children.top_down_role: Source-side encoding of aggregate balance deficits.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Source Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Super-source arcs for reducing balanced transshipment feasibility to maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0\), using the convention \(\partial x=d\). Create a new vertex \(s^*\). For every \(v\in V\) with \(d_v>0\), add an auxiliary arc \((s^*,v)\) with capacity \(d_v\); add no source arc when \(d_v\le0\). Retain every original arc and its capacity. Saturation of \((s^*,v)\) supplies the inflow needed for the original arcs to have net outflow \(d_v\) at \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a super-source arc of capacity equal to each positive supply, directing it into the corresponding supply vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The auxiliary-source arc set is \(A_{s^*}=\{(s^*,v):v\in V,\ d_v>0\}\), with capacity \(c_{s^*v}=d_v\) on each such arc.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Sink Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Super-sink arcs completing the transshipment-to-maximum-flow reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0\), using the convention \(\partial x=d\). Create a new vertex \(t^*\). For every \(v\in V\) with \(d_v<0\), add an auxiliary arc \((v,t^*)\) with capacity \(-d_v\); add no sink arc when \(d_v\ge0\). Retain every original arc and its capacity. Saturation of \((v,t^*)\) removes the excess inflow required at a demand vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add an arc from each demand vertex to a super-sink, with capacity equal to that vertex's demand magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The auxiliary-sink arc set is \(A_{t^*}=\{(v,t^*):v\in V,\ d_v<0\}\), with capacity \(c_{vt^*}=-d_v\) on each such arc.

children.title: Auxiliary-Arc Saturation Test
children.top_down_role: Feasibility interpretation attached to auxiliary terminal arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Arc Saturation Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-flow certificate for feasibility of a balanced zero-lower-bound transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with nonnegative capacities \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0\), using the balance convention \(\partial x=d\). Form the augmented network with arcs \((s^*,v)\) of capacity \(d_v\) for \(d_v>0\) and arcs \((v,t^*)\) of capacity \(-d_v\) for \(d_v<0\). Put \(D=\sum_{v\in V:d_v>0}d_v\). The original transshipment is feasible if and only if the augmented network admits an \(s^*\)-to-\(t^*\) flow of value \(D\). Equivalently, every arc leaving \(s^*\), and hence every arc entering \(t^*\), is saturated. Restricting such a flow to the original arcs certifies feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transshipment is feasible exactly when a maximum flow has total value equal to the total positive balance, thereby saturating every auxiliary source and sink arc.
assumptions_latex: The auxiliary arcs use the outflow-minus-inflow convention \(\partial x=d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to \(\operatorname{val}(x)=D\), equivalently to saturation of all auxiliary terminal arcs.

notation.meaning: total positive balance, equal to total demand magnitude

children.title: Flow-to-Circulation Reduction
children.top_down_role: Conversion of a source-sink flow instance into a circulation instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-to-Circulation Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Return-arc encoding of a capacitated source-sink flow as a circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(
u\) in \(G=(V,A)\), so conservation holds on \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), the net outflow at \(s\) is \(
u\), and the net inflow at \(t\) is \(
u\). Add a return arc \(e_0=(t,s)\) whose permitted interval contains \(
u\), and define \(f_a=x_a\) for \(a\in A\) and \(f_{e_0}=
u\). Then \(f\) is a circulation in the augmented graph. Thus fixing \(f_{e_0}=
u\) encodes the flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a return arc from sink to source carrying the flow value; the resulting augmented flow is a circulation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible capacitated \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(\nu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extending \(x\) by \(f_{(t,s)}=\nu\) produces a feasible circulation.

children.title: Circulation-to-Flow Recovery
children.top_down_role: Extraction of source-sink flow information from the circulation representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation-to-Flow Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a source-sink flow by deleting its value-encoding return arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and let \(G'=(V,A\cup\{e_0\})\) be the augmented graph with distinguished return arc \(e_0=(t,s)\). Let \(f\) be a feasible circulation on \(G'\), and put \(
u=f_{e_0}\). Delete \(e_0\) and define \(x_a=f_a\) for every \(a\in A\). Conservation of \(f\) implies that \(x\) has net outflow \(
u\) at \(s\), net inflow \(
u\) at \(t\), and zero balance at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\). If the bounds on arcs in \(A\) are the original bounds, then \(x\) is a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(
u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete the sink-to-source return arc; its circulation amount becomes the recovered source-sink flow value.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s,t\in V\) are distinct.
All arcs in \(A\) retain the original flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction \(x=f|_A\) is an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow with value \(\operatorname{val}(x)=f_{e_0}\).

notation.meaning: restriction of the circulation to original arcs

children.title: Value-Encoding Return Arc
children.top_down_role: Return-arc role in representing source-sink flow value.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Encoding Return Arc
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard reduction of a capacitated source-sink flow to a circulation by a return arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have source \(s\), sink \(t\), capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and let \(F\ge0\). Add an arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) with lower and upper bounds \(\ell(a_0)=u(a_0)=F\), leaving each original arc bounded by \(0\le x_e\le u_e\). Then restriction to \(E\) is a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(F\) if and only if the augmented vector is a feasible circulation. More generally, if \(0\le x_{a_0}\le U\), the return-arc value equals the value of the recovered flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed return flow from the sink to the source converts a flow of prescribed value into a circulation; the return-arc flow records that value.
assumptions_latex: All capacities are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x|_E\text{ has value }F\iff (x,x_{a_0}=F)\text{ is a feasible circulation}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locate Procedure on a Cut-Labeled Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subroutine acting on the cut-labeled tree \(T^{p-1}\) with target node p and deterministic edge tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(T\leftarrow T^{p-1}\). While \(T\) has more than one node, select its minimum-value edge \((\alpha,\beta)\), breaking ties by least order index. Let its associated cut partition \(N\) into \(N_\alpha,N_\beta\), with \(\alpha\in N_\alpha\) and \(\beta\in N_\beta\), and let deleting the edge partition \(T\) into \(T_\alpha,T_\beta\). Replace \(T\) by \(T_\alpha\) if \(p\in N_\alpha\), and by \(T_\beta\) otherwise. When \(T\) is a singleton, return its node as \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose the least-valued tree edge, use its associated cut to identify the side containing p, and retain the corresponding tree component. Return the sole remaining node k.
assumptions_latex: T^{p-1}\text{ is a tree whose edges have values, order indices, and associated cuts.}
\text{Each selected edge }(\alpha,\beta)\text{ induces components }T_\alpha,T_\beta\text{ and cut sides }N_\alpha,N_\beta.
\text{Ties are broken in favor of the least order index.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is the unique node remaining after the recursive restrictions.}

children.title: Transshipment-to-Circulation Reduction
children.top_down_role: Conversion of supply-demand balance data into a circulation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment-to-Circulation Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes prescribed vertex divergences as fixed flows incident to one auxiliary vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have bounds \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) and prescribed divergences \(b:V\to\mathbb R\), where \(\sum_{v\in V}b(v)=0\) and divergence means outgoing flow minus incoming flow. Add a vertex \(r\). For each \(v\) with \(b(v)>0\), add \((r,v)\) fixed at \(b(v)\); for each \(v\) with \(b(v)<0\), add \((v,r)\) fixed at \(-b(v)\). Then \(x\) is a bounded transshipment with divergence \(b\) exactly when its extension by these fixed arcs is a bounded circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary vertex and fixed incident arcs absorb every prescribed vertex imbalance, yielding an equivalent circulation instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Balance-Encoding Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-consistent interface between transshipment divergences and fixed auxiliary-arc flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt \(\operatorname{div}_x(v)=x(\delta^+(v))-x(\delta^-(v))\). A balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) is compatible with a closed transshipment instance precisely when \(\sum_{v\in V}b(v)=0\). Its circulation encoding must contribute auxiliary divergence \(-b(v)\) at every original vertex: use a fixed incoming arc of value \(b(v)\) when \(b(v)>0\), a fixed outgoing arc of value \(-b(v)\) when \(b(v)<0\), and no balance arc when \(b(v)=0\). Reversing the divergence convention reverses these arc orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balances must sum to zero, and each fixed auxiliary arc must contribute the negative of its vertex’s required divergence.
assumptions_latex: Divergence is defined as outgoing minus incoming flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V}b(v)=0\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{div}_{\mathrm{aux}}(v)=-b(v)\ \forall v\in V.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V^+,V^-;A)\) be bipartite, with \(s\in\mathbb R_+^{V^+}\) and \(d\in\mathbb R_+^{V^-}\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph and let $f,g:A\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $f\le g$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hoffman Feasibility Criterion with Variable Node Imbalances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the existence of an edge-bounded flow whose node imbalance vector may be selected within prescribed node bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D=(V,A)$ have edge bounds $f\le g$ and node bounds $f_V:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ and $g_V:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfying $f_V\le g_V$. Writing $\widetilde h(X)=\sum_{v\in X}h(v)$, there exist $m:V\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f_V\le m\le g_V$ and a feasible $m$-flow if and only if, for every $X\subseteq V$,
\[
\varrho_f(X)-\delta_g(X)\le \min\{-\widetilde f_V(V\setminus X),\widetilde g_V(X)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge-bounded flow with a node-imbalance vector lying between the prescribed node bounds exists exactly when every vertex subset satisfies the stated incoming-lower-bound versus outgoing-upper-bound inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\exists m:V\to\mathbb{R},\ f_V\le m\le g_V,\ \exists\text{ feasible }m\text{-flow}\right]\iff\left[\forall X\subseteq V,\ \varrho_f(X)-\delta_g(X)\le\min\{-\widetilde f_V(V\setminus X),\widetilde g_V(X)\}\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Circulation Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman’s finite directed bounded-circulation criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with real arc bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\). A circulation \(x\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) exists if and only if, for every subset \(S\subseteq V\),
\[
\ell(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S)).
\]
Here bounds are summed over the indicated cut arcs. Equivalently, no vertex set requires more lower-bounded inflow than its outgoing arcs can carry. The inequalities for \(S=\varnothing\) and \(S=V\) are vacuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded circulation exists exactly when every vertex set’s mandatory incoming flow is at most its available outgoing capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_a,u_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x:\operatorname{div}_x=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\iff \ell(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S))\ \forall S\subseteq V.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Repair for a Lower-Bounded Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteratively repairs arcs whose flow is below its lower bound while maintaining conservation and respecting two-sided residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with the zero circulation. While some arc $(p,q)$ has $x_{pq}<l_{pq}$, find a residual augmenting path from $q$ to $p$ whose forward arcs permit increases below capacity and whose backward arcs satisfy $x_{ij}>l_{ij}$. Augment by $\delta>0$ bounded by all residual slacks and by $l_{pq}-x_{pq}$. Repeat until every arc satisfies its lower bound; if the network admits a feasible circulation, this process obtains one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from zero. For an arc below its lower bound, send residual flow from its head back to its tail, never increasing a forward arc beyond capacity or decreasing a backward arc below its lower bound. Repeat for deficient arcs; when a feasible circulation exists, the procedure obtains one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\text{ produced by the augmentation process such that }\forall(i,j),\ l_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\text{ and flow is conserved at every node}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral residual-labeling procedure for repairing violated lower or upper arc bounds while preserving flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite directed network with integral bounds \(\ell(x,y)\le c(x,y)\), start from an integral flow \(f\) satisfying conservation at every node. While an arc \((s,t)\) violates a bound, perform the prescribed residual-labeling search for a correcting cycle through \((s,t)\). If breakthrough occurs, augment around that cycle by the admissible labeled amount; conservation and all previously satisfied arc bounds remain valid, while \(f(s,t)\) moves at least one unit toward \([\ell(s,t),c(s,t)]\). Repeat. The procedure terminates finitely either with \(\ell(x,y)\le f(x,y)\le c(x,y)\) on every arc or with a nonbreakthrough cut which, after orienting its sides appropriately, satisfies \[c(X,\bar X)<\ell(\bar X,X),\] certifying infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an integral conserved flow, residual labeling finds cycles that correct bound-violating arcs. Each successful correction preserves conservation and already satisfied bounds. Finitely many corrections yield a feasible circulation, or a failed search yields a cut proving that none exists.
assumptions_latex: \(f\text{ is initially integral and satisfies flow conservation at every node}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The procedure terminates finitely with either a feasible circulation or some }X\subseteq N\text{ such that }c(X,\bar X)<\ell(\bar X,X).\)

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Maximum-Flow Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tests lower-bounded circulation feasibility through one auxiliary maximum-flow computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((D,\ell,u)\), initialize \(x=\ell\), set residual capacities \(c_a=u_a-\ell_a\), and define \(b(v)=\ell(\delta^-(v))-\ell(\delta^+(v))\). Add a supersource \(p\) and supersink \(q\); add \((p,v)\) of capacity \(b(v)\) when \(b(v)>0\), and \((v,q)\) of capacity \(-b(v)\) when \(b(v)<0\). Compute a maximum \(p\)-\(q\) flow \(y\). Output \(x_a=\ell_a+y_a\) on original arcs if every arc leaving \(p\) is saturated; otherwise output infeasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Optimality Conditions for a Minimum-Cost Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual negative-circuit and potential certificates for a bounded feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $z$ be a feasible circulation with bounds $f\le z\le g$ and arc costs $c$. The following are equivalent: (i) $z$ has minimum cost; (ii) the residual digraph $D_z$ has no negative circuit with respect to $c_z$; (iii) there exists $\pi:V\to\mathbb R$ such that $\pi(v)-\pi(u)\le c(uv)$ whenever $z(uv)<g(uv)$ and $\pi(v)-\pi(u)\ge c(uv)$ whenever $z(uv)>f(uv)$. If $c$ is integral, $\pi$ may be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded feasible circulation is cheapest exactly when its residual network has no negative-cost directed circuit, equivalently when a vertex potential satisfies the appropriate reduced-cost inequalities on arcs that can be increased or decreased. Integral costs admit an integral potential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\text{ is minimum-cost}\iff D_z\text{ has no negative }c_z\text{-circuit}\iff \exists\pi\text{ satisfying the forward and backward residual inequalities};\quad c\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow\pi\in\mathbb Z^V\text{ may be chosen}.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Sink Flow Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated single-commodity flows with one source and one sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, and let \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\). With node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), whose arc columns have \(-1\) at the tail and \(+1\) at the head, the source-sink flow polyhedron is
\[P_{s,t}(u)=\{(f,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}: Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}.\]
Thus every intermediate node has zero net imbalance, the source has net outflow \(v\), and the sink has net inflow \(v\). Its projection onto arc variables is obtained by eliminating \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedron consists of capacity-feasible arc flows conserving flow at intermediate nodes and carrying a nonnegative common value from the designated source to the designated sink.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{s,t}(u)=\{(f,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}:Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}\).

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix with head entry +1 and tail entry -1.
Nonnegative value of the source-sink flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Source-Sink Flows and Associated Cut Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bounded directed source-sink flows, their value and maximum-flow formulation, the integral-optimum consequence for integral bounds, and the associated directed cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a loopless digraph with distinct vertices $v,w$. A $v$-$w$ flow is a vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{E(G)}$ satisfying $\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(u)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(u)}x_e=0$ for every $u\in V(G)\setminus\{v,w\}$. Given $l:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ and $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$, the flow is feasible if $l(e)\le x_e\le c(e)$ for every $e$. Its value satisfies $z(x):=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(v)}x_e=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(w)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(w)}x_e$. The maximum $v$-$w$ flow problem maximizes $z(x)$ over feasible flows and is a linear program. If all finite lower and upper bounds are integral, then an integer-valued optimal flow exists whenever an optimal solution exists. A $v$-$w$ cutset is a set $S\subset V(G)$ with $v\in S$ and $w\notin S$, with capacity $C(S):=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(S)}c(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(S)}l(e)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded source-sink flow conserves flow at every vertex except the distinct source and sink and respects the lower and upper arc bounds. Its net outflow from the source equals its net inflow to the sink. Maximum flow is the linear program maximizing this value; integral bounds yield an integral optimum whenever an optimum exists. A source-sink cut contains the source but not the sink, and its capacity is the sum of outgoing upper bounds minus the sum of incoming lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the integrality conclusion, every finite value of }l\text{ and }c\text{ is integral, and an optimal solution exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z(x)=\operatorname{netout}_v(x)=\operatorname{netin}_w(x);\quad \max\{z(x):x\text{ is feasible}\}\text{ is an LP; integral finite bounds admit an integral optimum when an optimum exists; and }C(S)=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(S)}c(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(S)}l(e).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Circulation Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circulations with lower and upper bounds on every arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell\leq u\). The bounded circulation polyhedron is
\[P_{\mathrm{circ}}(\ell,u)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:Bf=0,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}.\]
The equation \(Bf=0\) imposes flow conservation at every node, while the componentwise inequalities impose the prescribed arc bounds. The polyhedron may be empty; when it is nonempty and both bound vectors are integral, every vertex is integral because the defining network matrix is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded circulation obeys flow conservation at every node and lies between prescribed lower and upper arc bounds; integral bounds give integral vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{circ}}(\ell,u)=\{f:Bf=0,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\), with integral vertices when \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated network flows realizing a prescribed node-balance vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\). For a balance vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), and bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) with \(\ell\leq u\), the transshipment polyhedron is
\[P(b,\ell,u)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}.\]
Under the incidence convention used here, positive \(b_v\) denotes net inflow demand and negative \(b_v\) denotes net supply. If \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, every vertex of a nonempty polyhedron \(P(b,\ell,u)\) is integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Side Optimization Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming formulation of the maximum source-sink flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), distinct nodes \(s,t\), capacities \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\), and incidence matrix \(B\), the maximum-flow problem has the linear-programming representation
\[\max\{v:(f,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R},\ Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}.\]
The scalar \(v\) is the net outflow from \(s\), equivalently the net inflow into \(t\). Feasibility enforces conservation at every node outside \(\{s,t\}\), and maximizing \(v\) selects a feasible source-sink flow of greatest value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow is a linear program maximizing the common source outflow and sink inflow subject to conservation and capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max v\) subject to \(Bf=v(e_t-e_s)\) and \(0\leq f\leq u\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Side Dual Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-form linear dual of the maximum-flow program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the maximum-flow assumptions, assign a potential \(p_v\) to each node and a nonnegative variable \(z_a\) to each arc. A cut-side dual model is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}u_a z_a:p_s=0,\ p_t=1,\ z_a\geq p_{\operatorname{head}(a)}-p_{\operatorname{tail}(a)},\ z_a\geq0\right\}.\]
Its optimum equals the maximum-flow value. An optimal potential may be chosen as the indicator of a set \(V\setminus S\), where \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\); then \(z\) indicates arcs leaving \(S\), and the objective is the capacity \(u(\delta^{+}(S))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flow LP dual minimizes weighted potential increases; an optimal binary potential identifies an source-sink cut whose capacity equals maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{v:Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}=\min_{s\in S,\ t\notin S}u(\delta^{+}(S))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Flow-Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual optimality certificate using a feasible flow and a saturated cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be a feasible source-sink flow of value \(v\), and let \(S\subseteq V\) satisfy \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\). The pair \((f,S)\) certifies simultaneous flow and cut optimality if
\[f_a=u_a\quad(a\in\delta^{+}(S)),\qquad f_a=0\quad(a\in\delta^{-}(S)).\]
Flow conservation then gives
\[v=f(\delta^{+}(S))-f(\delta^{-}(S))=u(\delta^{+}(S)).\]
Every feasible flow has value at most every source-sink cut capacity, so this equality is directly checkable and certifies that \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and cut are jointly optimal when every forward cut arc is saturated and every reverse cut arc carries zero flow.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible source-sink flow of value \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v=u(\delta^{+}(S))\), so \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is a minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Arc Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed incidence representation of conservation in a finite loopless directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite loopless directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), its node-arc incidence matrix is \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\) defined for an arc \(a=(i,j)\), where \(i\neq j\), by
\[B_{va}=\begin{cases}-1,&v=i,\\+1,&v=j,\\0,&v\notin\{i,j\}.\end{cases}\]
Consequently, for any arc vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), the coordinate \((Bf)_v\) equals total inflow to \(v\) minus total outflow from \(v\). Every column sums to zero, and if the underlying undirected graph has \(k\) connected components, then \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite loopless directed graph, an incidence column has minus one at an arc's tail and plus one at its distinct head, so matrix multiplication records node imbalance.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite loopless directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Bf)_v\) is net inflow at \(v\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-k\).

notation.meaning: Number of connected components of the underlying undirected graph.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard signed-incidence definition and rank formula for loopless directed graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Unimodularity Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of network-flow polyhedra derived from total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The node-arc incidence matrix \(B\) of every directed graph is totally unimodular: every square subdeterminant belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). Appending unit rows and changing row signs preserves total unimodularity, so the constraint matrix formed from \(B\), \(-B\), \(I\), and \(-I\) is totally unimodular. Therefore, if \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, every vertex of
\[\{f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\]
is integral whenever this polyhedron is nonempty. This supplies the total-unimodularity route to integrality for circulations, transshipments, and source-sink flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed incidence matrices are totally unimodular; hence network-flow polyhedra with integral balances and bounds have only integral vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the node-arc incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{f:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\) is an integral polyhedron when nonempty.

notation.meaning: Identity matrix indexed by the arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Dual-Integrality Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-polyhedron integrality obtained through integral optimal dual solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the bounded network system \(Bf=b\), \(\ell\leq f\leq u\) as inequalities using \(Bf\leq b\), \(-Bf\leq-b\), \(f\leq u\), and \(-f\leq-\ell\). This system is totally dual integral: for every integral objective \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) whose primal maximum is finite, the linear-programming dual has an integral optimal multiplier vector. When \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, total dual integrality implies that the associated polyhedron is integral. Thus integral optimal flows and integral dual certificates can be selected for all bounded integral network-flow instances with finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded network-flow inequality system is totally dual integral, yielding integral primal vertices and integral optimal dual certificates for integral data.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a directed node-arc incidence matrix.
\(b,\ell,u\) and the optimized objective vector are integral.
The relevant primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded network system is TDI, and integral right-hand sides yield an integral polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-flow algorithm for networks with nonnegative integral capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f(e)=0$ for every $e\in E(G)$. While the residual graph $G_f$ contains an $s$-$t$ path $P$, set $\gamma=\min_{a\in E(P)}u_f(a)$ and augment $f$ along $P$ by $\gamma$. When no augmenting path remains, return $f$; for integral capacities the procedure terminates with a maximum $s$-$t$ flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow and repeatedly augment by the bottleneck residual capacity of any residual source-to-sink path. With integral capacities, the process terminates and returns a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, }f\text{ is a maximum }s\text{-}t\text{ flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Labeling Search for an Augmenting Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual reachability relative to a feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the labeled-but-unscanned set as \(I=\{s\}\). While \(I\neq\varnothing\) and \(t\notin I\), remove a node \(i\in I\) for scanning. knowledge_statements.title: Generic Augmenting-Path Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ford-Fulkerson with an arbitrary residual source-sink path rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed network \(D=(V,A)\), distinct \(s,t\), and capacities \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\). Initialize \(f=0\). Given feasible \(f\), form the residual network with forward residual capacity \(u_a-f_a\) and reverse residual capacity \(f_a\). If it contains an \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(P\), set \(\Delta=\min_{e\in P}r_e\), increase \(f_a\) by \(\Delta\) on forward occurrences, decrease it by \(\Delta\) on reverse occurrences, and repeat. If no such path exists, output \(f\) and the set \(S\) of vertices reachable from \(s\); then \((f,S)\) is a maximum-flow/minimum-cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment along any residual source-sink path by its bottleneck capacity; when no path remains, return the maximum flow and reachable minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the method stops, its output \(f\) is maximum and the residual reachable set \(S\) is a minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Capacity Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of arbitrary Ford-Fulkerson augmentations for integer capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let all arc capacities be nonnegative integers, initialize the Ford-Fulkerson method with the zero flow, and choose any residual source-sink path at each iteration. Every residual capacity and every augmentation amount \(\Delta\) remains integral; hence each augmentation increases the flow value by at least \(1\). If \(F^{*}\) denotes the maximum-flow value, the algorithm performs at most \(F^{*}\) augmentations and terminates with a maximum flow. The same conclusion holds from any integral feasible initial flow, with at most \(F^{*}-v_0\) augmentations when its initial value is \(v_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integer capacities and an integral initial flow, every augmentation raises flow value by at least one, so arbitrary Ford-Fulkerson path choices terminate.
assumptions_latex: The initial feasible flow is integral.
Each iteration chooses a residual source-sink path when one exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates after at most \(F^{*}-v_0\) augmentations and returns a maximum flow.

notation.meaning: Value of the initial integral feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Value-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudopolynomial running-time bound for integral-capacity Ford-Fulkerson.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume integer capacities, the zero initial flow, adjacency-list storage, and a path search requiring \(O(|V|+|A|)\) time. Since every Ford-Fulkerson augmentation increases the flow value by at least \(1\), at most \(F^{*}\) augmentations occur. The total running time is therefore
\[O\bigl((|V|+|A|)F^{*}\bigr),\]
or \(O(|A|F^{*})\) when every relevant vertex is incident to an arc. This bound is pseudopolynomial: \(F^{*}\) can be exponentially large in the binary encoding length of the capacities, so it is not a polynomial bound in the input bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ford-Fulkerson with integer capacities takes at most the maximum-flow value many augmentations, giving pseudopolynomial time proportional to path-search cost times that value.
assumptions_latex: Capacities are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
The algorithm starts from zero flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(O((|V|+|A|)F^{*})\), which is pseudopolynomial in binary input size.

knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Capacity Nontermination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of arbitrary Ford–Fulkerson path selection with nonnegative real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite directed network have source \(s\), sink \(t\), and capacities \(u_e\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). Ford–Fulkerson repeatedly selects any residual \(s\)-\(t\) path and augments by its bottleneck residual capacity. If all capacities are integral, every positive augmentation increases the flow value by at least one; this termination mechanism disappears for irrational capacities. There exist networks with irrational capacities and admissible infinite path-selection sequences whose augmentation amounts tend to zero, so the generated feasible flows never attain a maximum flow and their values may converge to a value strictly below the maximum-flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Irrational capacities permit infinite Ford–Fulkerson augmentation sequences with vanishing increments, potentially converging below the maximum-flow value.
assumptions_latex: Augmenting paths may be selected arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Ford--Fulkerson need not terminate, and }\lim_k |f_k|<|f^*|\text{ can occur.}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest Augmenting-Path Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-length shortest residual paths, including the Edmonds–Karp selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible flow \(f\) in a finite capacitated network with source \(s\) and sink \(t\). At iteration \(k\), assign length one to every arc of the residual graph \(G_{f_k}\), find an \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P_k\) having the fewest arcs, and set \(\delta_k=\min_{e\in P_k}u_{f_k}(e)\). Augment \(f_k\) by \(\delta_k\) along \(P_k\), including the usual cancellation on reverse residual arcs. Stop and output \(f_k\) when no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists; the output is then a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment along a residual path with the fewest arcs; absence of such a path certifies maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and all capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_k\in\arg\min_P |P|\), and termination returns a maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Capacity Augmenting-Path Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Widest-path selection by maximum residual bottleneck capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow \(f_k\), define the width of a residual \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) by \(b_{f_k}(P)=\min_{e\in P}u_{f_k}(e)\). Select a widest augmenting path \(P_k\in\arg\max_P b_{f_k}(P)\), augment by \(b_{f_k}(P_k)\), and update forward and reverse residual capacities. A widest path may be found by labeling \(s\) with \(+\infty\), repeatedly giving each vertex the largest achievable bottleneck label, and stopping when \(t\) is finalized. If no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists, output the current flow as maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every iteration, augment along a residual path whose bottleneck capacity is largest among all residual source–sink paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_{f_k}(P_k)=\max_P\min_{e\in P}u_{f_k}(e)\).

notation.meaning: widest residual path at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Based Path Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a residual path from exact distance-price labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a residual graph \(G_f\), source \(s\), sink \(t\), and labels \(p(v)\) equal to the minimum number of residual arcs from \(v\) to \(t\), with \(p(v)=+\infty\) when \(t\) is unreachable. If \(p(s)=+\infty\), report that no augmenting path exists. Otherwise initialize \(v=s\) and an empty path. While \(v\ne t\), choose a residual arc \((v,w)\) satisfying \(p(v)=p(w)+1\), append it, and replace \(v\) by \(w\). Output the resulting simple \(s\)-\(t\) path and augment by its residual bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow residual arcs whose price labels decrease by one; exact distance labels guarantee arrival at the sink along a shortest path.
assumptions_latex: \(p(v)\) is the residual arc distance from \(v\) to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(s)<+\infty\) implies construction of an augmenting path \(P\) with \(|P|=p(s)\).

notation.meaning: distance-price label from v to the sink

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintains a simple forward path and integer node prices while seeking an s-to-t path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed graph with $N=|\mathcal N|$ and specified nodes $s,t$. Initialize $P=(s)$ and integer prices satisfying $p_i\le p_j+1$ for every $(i,j)\in\mathcal A$, $p_s<N$, and $p_t=0$. Maintain a simple path $P=(s,n_1,\ldots,n_k)$ satisfying $p_i\ge p_j$ on every path arc. At the endpoint $n_k$, if $N(n_k)=\varnothing$, set $p_{n_k}=N$ and proceed to contraction. Otherwise select $\operatorname{succ}(n_k)\in\arg\min_{j\in N(n_k)}p_j$ and set $p_{n_k}=p_{\operatorname{succ}(n_k)}+1$. Extend to this successor if $n_k=s$ or $p_{\operatorname{pred}(n_k)}>p_{\operatorname{succ}(n_k)}$; otherwise contract by deleting the last path arc. Stop with the maintained path when an extension reaches $t$, or stop with the no-path outcome when $P=(s)$ and $p_s\ge N$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting with the singleton path at s, repeatedly relabel its endpoint from the minimum-price outgoing neighbor. Extend when the price test permits and otherwise delete the last path arc. Stop upon reaching t or when the singleton source path has source price at least the number of nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated stopping outcomes are an }s\text{-}t\text{ forward path upon reaching }t\text{ and the no-path report when }P=(s),\ p_s\ge N.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses repeated price-based path construction in the reduced graph, retaining valid prices between augmentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Begin with a capacity-feasible flow and, for example, the zero price vector. Repeatedly apply the price-based path construction algorithm to the current reduced graph to obtain an $s$-$t$ path and augment the flow along it. Prices satisfy $p_i\le p_j+1$ on every reduced-graph arc and may remain unchanged after augmentation: every newly created reverse arc $(j,i)$ corresponds to a path arc $(i,j)$ with $p_i\ge p_j$, hence satisfies $p_j\le p_i+1$. Continue until the path construction algorithm reports that no $s$-$t$ path exists. A suitable variant admits complexity $O(N^2A)$, where $N$ and $A$ are the numbers of nodes and original arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method repeatedly finds an augmenting path in the current reduced graph with the price-based path procedure and augments the flow. Its node prices remain valid after each augmentation and can be reused. A suitable variant runs in order N squared times A.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is an initial capacity-feasible flow}
p_i\le p_j+1\quad\text{for every arc }(i,j)\text{ of the current reduced graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Repeated price-based reduced-graph augmentations form a Ford--Fulkerson-type max-flow algorithm, with persistent valid prices; a suitable variant has complexity }O(N^2A).

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Label Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bellman consistency conditions for residual distance-price labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual graph \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) and sink \(t\), a distance-price labeling is a map \(p:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfying \(p(t)=0\) and, for every \(v\ne t\), \[p(v)=\min_{(v,w)\in E_f}\bigl(1+p(w)\bigr),\] where the minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\). After an augmentation changes \(E_f\), labels are maintained by applying these Bellman updates until every vertex again satisfies the displayed equality. A finite label then equals the minimum number of residual arcs from that vertex to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Price labels satisfy residual Bellman equations and are updated after augmentation until they again equal distances to the sink.
assumptions_latex: Every residual arc has unit length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(v,t)\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: price or distance label of vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-distance properties of successive shortest augmenting paths in Edmonds–Karp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f_1,f_2,\ldots$ be flows such that $f_{i+1}$ results from $f_i$ by augmentation along a shortest $f_i$-augmenting path $P_i$. Then $|E(P_k)|\leq |E(P_{k+1})|$ for every $k$. Moreover, for every $k<l$ such that $P_k\cup P_l$ contains a pair of reverse edges, $|E(P_k)|+2\leq |E(P_l)|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For successive augmentations along shortest augmenting paths, path lengths never decrease. If an earlier and a later path together contain a pair of reverse edges, the later path is at least two edges longer.
assumptions_latex: f_{i+1}\text{ results from }f_i\text{ by augmentation along }P_i.
P_i\text{ is a shortest }f_i\text{-augmenting path for every }i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k,\ |E(P_k)|\leq |E(P_{k+1})|,\qquad \forall k<l,\ \bigl(P_k\cup P_l\text{ contains a pair of reverse edges}\bigr)\Rightarrow |E(P_k)|+2\leq |E(P_l)|.

knowledge_statements.title: Breadth-First Residual Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Breadth-first implementation of Edmonds–Karp path selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the residual graph \(G_f\), initialize a first-in-first-out queue with \(s\), set \(d(s)=0\), and leave all other vertices undiscovered. Repeatedly remove the queue head \(v\); for each residual arc \((v,w)\) with \(w\) undiscovered, set \(d(w)=d(v)+1\), record predecessor \(v\), and enqueue \(w\). If \(t\) is discovered, predecessor pointers recover an \(s\)-\(t\) residual path with the fewest arcs. If the queue empties without discovering \(t\), no augmenting path exists and the current feasible flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Breadth-first search finds a minimum-arc residual augmenting path or certifies that none exists.
assumptions_latex: All residual arcs are assigned unit length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(t)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,t)\), or \(t\) is unreachable from \(s\).

notation.meaning: residual graph of the current flow

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds–Karp bound independent of capacity magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with \(n=|V|\) vertices and \(m=|E|\) original arcs, Edmonds–Karp performs \(O(nm)\) augmentations. A breadth-first residual search and the corresponding augmentation require \(O(m)\) arithmetic operations under an adjacency-list representation. Consequently, the algorithm computes a maximum flow in \(O(nm^2)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(n+m)\) working storage. The operation count depends only polynomially on \(n\) and \(m\), not on capacity values or their encoding lengths, so this is a strongly polynomial bound in the arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edmonds–Karp uses at most order nm augmentations and order nm² arithmetic operations, independently of capacity magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: Residual breadth-first search uses adjacency lists.
Exact arithmetic operations have unit cost.
