knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an arbitrary root \(r\). For each \(v\ne r\), compute or implicitly expose a minimum directed \(r\)-to-\(v\) cut and a minimum directed \(v\)-to-\(r\) cut, reusing contractions and flow information when available. Return the least-capacity exposed cut. The governing identity is
\[\lambda(D)=\min_{v\ne r}\min\{\lambda_D(r,v),\lambda_D(v,r)\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing one root reduces directed global minimum cut to rooted cuts in both directions. Hao-Orlin organizes these related computations so flow and contraction information can be reused.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Form the quotient \(D/\mathcal{P}\) by replacing each block by one vertex, deleting internal arcs, and assigning every quotient arc \((P,Q)\) capacity equal to the total capacity of arcs directed from \(P\) to \(Q\). If \(S\subseteq V\) is a union of blocks, then
\[c_D(\delta_D^+(S))=c_{D/\mathcal{P}}(\delta_{D/\mathcal{P}}^+(\pi(S))).\]
Consequently, quotient cuts correspond exactly, with preserved capacities, to original cuts that do not separate vertices within a block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting vertex blocks preserves exactly the capacities of directed cuts that are unions of whole blocks; quotient cuts lift canonically to the original graph.

After constructing \(D_{i+1}=D_i/\mathcal{P}_i\), set \(s_{i+1}=\pi_i(s_i)\) and perform a directed search from \(s_{i+1}\) using the aggregated quotient arcs. Store

Let \(f\) be a maximum \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow and let \(R\) contain precisely the vertices reachable from \(s\) in the residual graph \(D_f\). Then \(s\in R\), \(t\notin R\), and
\[c(\delta^+(R))=|f|=\lambda_D(s,t).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A capacitated tree is $K$-flow-equivalent to $G$ if it has the value property
\[\lambda_G(r,s)=\min_{e\in P_T(r,s)}f_e\qquad(r,s\in K).\]
If it also has the property that deleting a path edge attaining this minimum yields a corresponding minimum $(r,s)$-cut in $G$, it is a Gomory--Hu $K$-cut-tree. When $K=V$, the qualifier $K$ is omitted. A flow-equivalent tree need not be a cut-tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A K-flow-equivalent tree preserves every terminal-pair minimum-cut value as the smallest label on the corresponding tree path. A Gomory–Hu K-cut-tree additionally recovers a realizing cut by deleting a minimum-label path edge. The K qualifier is omitted when all vertices are terminals, and flow equivalence alone does not imply the cut-tree property.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gomory–Hu cut tree and all-pairs minimum-cut representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a Gomory–Hu tree and records its minimum-cut recovery and flow-equivalence properties for undirected capacitated graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb Q_+\). A Gomory--Hu tree is a tree \(T=(V,F)\) on the same vertex set such that, for every \(ij\in F\), the cut \(C_{ij}\) of \(G\) induced by the two components of \(T-ij\) is a minimum \([i,j]\)-cut in \(G\). Set \(d_{ij}=c(C_{ij})\); it is not required that \(F\subseteq E\). For any \(r,s\in V\), selecting an edge \(ij\) of minimum \(d_{ij}\) on the unique \([r,s]\)-path in \(T\) yields a minimum \([r,s]\)-cut \(C_{ij}\) in \(G\). Consequently, \(G\) and the capacitated tree \((T,d)\) have the same maximum-flow value for every vertex pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gomory–Hu tree is a tree on the vertices of an undirected capacitated graph whose edge-induced partitions are corresponding minimum cuts. A minimum-capacity tree edge on the path between any two vertices identifies a minimum cut for that pair, so the capacitated tree preserves all pairwise maximum-flow values. Tree edges need not be graph edges.
assumptions_latex: T=(V,F)\text{ is a tree satisfying the Gomory--Hu cut condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall r,s\in V,\quad \lambda_G(r,s)=\min\{d_{ij}:ij\in P_T(r,s)\}=\lambda_{(T,d)}(r,s),\quad\text{and every minimizing }ij\text{ yields a minimum }[r,s]\text{-cut }C_{ij}\text{ in }G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative construction for a capacitated graph and designated terminal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose terminals $r,s\in K$, compute a minimum $(r,s)$-cut with shores $R,S$, and initialize a tree whose nodes are $R,S$ and whose joining edge is labeled by the cut capacity. At a later stage, if a tree node $A$ contains terminals $y,z\in K$, form $G_A$ by identifying, separately, the vertices represented by each component of $T-A$. Compute a minimum $(y,z)$-cut in $G_A$, split $A$ into its shores $Y,Z$, join $Y$ and $Z$ by an edge labeled by that cut's capacity, and reattach each former neighbor of $A$ to the shore containing its identified vertex; retain all old edge labels. Continue until every tree node contains exactly one terminal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with a minimum cut between two terminals. Repeatedly split a tree part containing two terminals by a minimum cut after separately identifying the external tree components. Add the corresponding labeled edge, reattach neighboring parts according to their cut shores, and retain existing labels. Stop when every tree part contains one terminal.

\text{a selected tree part contains two terminal nodes}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Polynomial Construction of Gomory–Hu Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and recursive minimum-cut construction for undirected graphs with nonnegative capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge capacities has a Gomory--Hu tree. Such a tree can be found in polynomial time by recursively choosing $|V|-1$ noncrossing cuts, each new cut being a minimum cut for a pair of vertices not separated by the previously chosen cuts. Vertices $i,j$ are adjacent in the resulting tree if and only if exactly one chosen cut separates them, and the tree-edge weight $d_{ij}$ is the capacity of that cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every undirected graph with nonnegative edge capacities has a Gomory–Hu tree. It can be found in polynomial time from |V|−1 recursively chosen noncrossing minimum cuts. Two vertices are adjacent in the tree exactly when precisely one chosen cut separates them, and that edge is weighted by the cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a Gomory--Hu tree constructible in polynomial time from }|V|-1\text{ recursively selected noncrossing minimum cuts.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a cut-equivalent tree by recursively splitting vertex blocks with contracted minimum cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a block tree with the single block \(V(G)\). While a block \(X\) has \(|X|\geq2\), choose distinct \(s,t\in X\); contract, for every component \(C\) of the current tree minus \(X\), the union of the blocks in \(C\); compute a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut \((A',B')\) in the contracted graph; lift it to a partition \((A,B)\) of \(V(G)\); replace \(X\) by \(A\cap X\) and \(B\cap X\); reconnect each former neighbor of \(X\) to the side containing it; and join the two new blocks by an edge weighted with the computed cut capacity. When every block is a singleton, replace singleton blocks by their vertices. The resulting weighted tree \(T\) is a Gomory-Hu tree for \((G,u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with one block containing all vertices. Repeatedly choose two vertices in a nonsingleton block, contract the vertex unions represented by every component attached to that block, find a minimum cut between the chosen vertices, lift the cut, split the block, preserve and redirect its incident tree edges according to the cut sides, and add a new edge weighted by the cut capacity. When all blocks are singletons, the resulting tree is a Gomory-Hu tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a Gomory-Hu tree for }(G,u).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected graphs with nonnegative edge capacities; the representing tree has the same vertex set but need not be a subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be an undirected graph with $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+$, and let $T$ be a tree with $V(T)=V(G)$. For $e=xy\in E(T)$, let $C_e$ be the cut of $G$ induced by deleting $e$ from $T$. The tree $T$ is cut-equivalent to $(G,c)$ if every $C_e$ is a minimum-capacity $x$--$y$ cut in $G$. Given $c':E(T)\to\mathbb{R}_+$, $(T,c')$ is flow-equivalent to $(G,c)$ if, for every $x,y\in V(G)$, their maximum-flow values in $G$ and $T$ coincide. If $T$ is cut-equivalent and $c'(e)=\operatorname{cap}_G(C_e)$ for every $e\in E(T)$, then $(T,c')$ is flow-equivalent; the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree on the graph's vertex set is cut-equivalent when each tree edge induces a minimum cut between its endpoints in the original graph. A capacitated tree is flow-equivalent when it preserves every pairwise maximum-flow value. Assigning each edge of a cut-equivalent tree the capacity of its induced cut makes it flow-equivalent, but flow equivalence alone does not imply cut equivalence.
assumptions_latex: c':E(T)\to\mathbb{R}_+\text{ when flow equivalence is considered}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is cut-equivalent as defined above, }(T,c')\text{ is flow-equivalent as defined above, and }\bigl[T\text{ cut-equivalent},\ c'(e)=\operatorname{cap}_G(C_e)\bigr]\Rightarrow (T,c')\text{ flow-equivalent, but not conversely.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-tree nonuniqueness and uniqueness after generic perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness and a generic uniqueness boundary for Gomory–Hu cut trees of connected undirected capacitated networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A connected undirected capacitated network may admit more than one cut tree. After a sufficiently small lexicographic perturbation of edge capacities that makes all cut capacities distinct, the cut tree is unique. Its relevant \(n-1\) cuts determine adjacency: vertices \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent exactly when precisely one of those cuts separates them, and their tree edge has that cut's capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connected undirected network can have multiple cut trees. A sufficiently small generic perturbation that gives every cut a distinct capacity yields a unique cut tree, whose relevant n−1 cuts determine its edges and edge capacities.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected undirected capacitated network}
\text{for the uniqueness conclusion, capacities are perturbed so that all cut capacities are distinct}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Cut trees may be nonunique in general; under the stated perturbation, the cut tree is unique and determined by its }n-1\text{ relevant cuts.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree representation when the global minimum-cut value is odd
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-connectivity specialization of global minimum-cut cactus encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph whose minimum cut cardinality $k$ is odd. Then there exist a tree $H=(U,F)$ and a map $\varphi:V\to U$ such that the minimum cuts of $G$ correspond bijectively to the edges of $H$: for every $e\in F$, if $U_1,U_2$ are the vertex sets of the two components of $H-e$, then $\varphi^{-1}(U_1)$ and $\varphi^{-1}(U_2)$ are the shores of the corresponding minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists H=(U,F)\text{ a tree},\ \exists\varphi:V\to U\text{ inducing a bijection between }F\text{ and the minimum cuts of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cactus representation of all global minimum cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal cactus encoding theorem for global minimum cuts of a loopless graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $k\ge 1$ and let $G=(V,E)$ be a loopless graph whose minimum cut cardinality is $k$. There exist a cactus $C=(U,F)$ and a map $\varphi:V\to U$ such that, for every two-edge cut of $C$ with shores $U_1,U_2$, the sets $\varphi^{-1}(U_1)$ and $\varphi^{-1}(U_2)$ are the shores of a minimum cut of $G$, and every minimum cut of $G$ arises in this way. Equivalently, $X$ is tight in $G$ if and only if $\varphi(X)$ is tight in $C$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every loopless graph admits a cactus encoding of all its global minimum cuts. Each two-edge cut of the cactus pulls back to a minimum cut of the original graph, every original minimum cut is represented, and tight sets correspond under the mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C=(U,F)\text{ a cactus},\ \exists\varphi:V\to U:\quad X\text{ is tight in }G\iff \varphi(X)\text{ is tight in }C,\text{ and the two-edge cuts of }C\text{ represent exactly all minimum cuts of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c(\delta_G(S))\). In a cactus representation \((K,\phi)\), deleting a bridge of \(K\), or deleting two distinct edges belonging to one cycle of \(K\), produces two cactus components. The inverse image under \(\phi\) of either component is a side of a cut of capacity \(\lambda\). Conversely, every cut of capacity \(\lambda\) is obtained by one of these deletions. Thus all global-minimum-cut queries reduce to enumerating the relevant bridge and same-cycle edge-pair separations, with complementary sides identified as the same cut.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(G\). Compute its global minimum-cut value \(\lambda\), maintain a contracted graph \(G'\), and repeatedly expose a cut of value \(\lambda\) that separates two current blocks. Record the induced split, contract each side when processing the other, and recurse until no unresolved pair of blocks is separated by a minimum cut. Combine compatible splits as cactus bridges and combine crossing minimum cuts as cycles; suppress redundant unlabeled degree-two vertices and define \(\phi\) from each original vertex to its final block. Output \((K,\phi)\) only when every bridge and same-cycle edge pair induces a minimum cut and every minimum cut of \(G\) is represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cactus constructions recursively expose minimum cuts, contract resolved blocks, encode compatible cuts by bridges and crossing cuts by cycles, then verify completeness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and immediate boundary cases for solid vertex sets in an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, and let \(d_G(X)\) denote the size of the cut determined by \(X\subseteq V\). A nonempty set \(Z\subseteq V\) is solid (or extreme) if \(d_G(X)>d_G(Z)\) for every nonempty proper subset \(X\subset Z\). Every singleton is solid, and \(V\) is solid if and only if \(G\) is connected. A solid set \(Z\) is proper if \(Z\subset V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an undirected graph, a nonempty vertex set is solid, or extreme, when every nonempty proper subset has a strictly larger cut boundary. Every singleton is solid, the whole vertex set is solid exactly when the graph is connected, and a solid set is proper when it is strictly contained in the vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z\text{ is solid}\iff \forall X\,(\varnothing\ne X\subset Z\Rightarrow d_G(X)>d_G(Z));\quad |Z|=1\Rightarrow Z\text{ is solid};\quad V\text{ is solid}\iff G\text{ is connected}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by separation between internal and external pairwise edge-connectivity values, including the whole-graph convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and let \(\lambda_G(u,v)\) denote the edge-connectivity between vertices \(u\) and \(v\). A nonempty set \(K\subseteq V\) is a \(\lambda\)-component of \(G\) if
\[\min\{\lambda_G(u,v):u,v\in K\}>\max\{\lambda_G(u,v):u\in K,\ v\in V\setminus K\}.\]
The minimum on the left is called the edge-connectivity of \(K\). By convention, if \(G\) is connected, then \(V\) is a \(\lambda\)-component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty vertex set is a lambda-component when its minimum internal pairwise edge-connectivity is strictly greater than its maximum pairwise edge-connectivity to vertices outside the set. The internal minimum is the edge-connectivity of the component. By convention, the full vertex set of a connected graph is a lambda-component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-component}\iff \min_{u,v\in K}\lambda_G(u,v)>\max_{u\in K,\,v\in V\setminus K}\lambda_G(u,v),\quad \lambda(K):=\min_{u,v\in K}\lambda_G(u,v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut, tight-set, crossing, and cross-free terminology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for undirected cuts and crossing families used in global minimum-cut structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be connected. For $\varnothing\subset X\subset V$, $\Delta(X)$ is the set of edges joining $X$ to $V\setminus X$, whose shores are $X$ and $V\setminus X$; equality $\Delta(X)=\Delta(Y)$ implies $Y=X$ or $Y=V\setminus X$. A cut is a star-cut if one shore is a singleton and is proper otherwise. Sets $X,Y\subseteq V$ cross when each of $X\setminus Y$, $Y\setminus X$, $X\cap Y$, and $V\setminus(X\cup Y)$ is nonempty; their cuts cross when their shores cross. In a $k$-edge-connected graph, a cut of cardinality $k$ is a min-cut, $T\subset V$ is tight when $d(T)=k$, and a tight set is proper when neither shore is a singleton. A set family is cross-free when no two members cross.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a connected graph, a cut is the edge boundary of a nonempty proper vertex set, and it determines its two shores up to complementation. Star-cuts have a singleton shore; all other cuts are proper. Two vertex sets cross when all four regions determined by them are nonempty, and cuts cross when their shores do. In a k-edge-connected graph, cuts of size k are minimum cuts, their shores are tight sets, and a family is cross-free if no two members cross.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta(X)=\Delta(Y)\Rightarrow Y\in\{X,V\setminus X\},\quad \mathcal F\text{ is cross-free}\iff \forall X,Y\in\mathcal F,\ X\text{ and }Y\text{ do not cross.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersecting and crossing families and restricted submodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both family classes, records their inclusions and transformations, and characterizes crossing families by lattice-family slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A family $\mathcal C\subseteq2^E$ is intersecting if $S,T\in\mathcal C$ and $S\cap T
eq\varnothing$ imply $S\cap T,S\cup T\in\mathcal C$. It is crossing if the same conclusion is required whenever additionally $S\cup T
eq E$. Thus every lattice family is intersecting and every intersecting family is crossing. For $i,j\in E$, let $\mathcal C_{ij}:=\{T\in\mathcal C:i\in T,1j
otin T\}$. Then $\mathcal C$ is crossing iff every $\mathcal C_{ij}$ is a lattice family; together with separate membership bits for $\varnothing$ and $E$, these slices give a polynomial-space encoding. A function $f:\mathcal C	o\mathbb R$ is submodular on intersecting pairs, respectively crossing pairs, when $$f(S\cap T)+f(S\cup T)\leq f(S)+f(T)$$ for every qualifying intersecting, respectively crossing, pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting families are closed under union and intersection for pairs with nonempty intersection; crossing families impose this only when the union is also not the ground set. Lattice families are intersecting, and intersecting families are crossing. A family is crossing exactly when every slice separating an ordered pair of elements is a lattice family, which yields a compact encoding. Submodularity may correspondingly be required only on the qualifying pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C\text{ is crossing}\iff\forall i,j\in E,\ \mathcal C_{ij}\text{ is a lattice family}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone and symmetric reductions of the orientation criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two special cases in which the general pair of partition conditions reduces to a single family of inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(h:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be crossing \(G\)-supermodular with \(h(\varnothing)=h(V)=0\). If \(h\) is non-increasing, then \(G\) has an orientation covering \(h\) whenever \[e_G(\mathcal P)\ge\sum_{X\in\mathcal P}h(X)\] for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) with at least two blocks. If \(h\) is symmetric, it suffices to impose this inequality only on two-block partitions; equivalently, it suffices that \[d_G(X)\ge2h(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\subset V.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a non-increasing crossing-supermodular requirement, the block-side partition inequality alone guarantees a covering orientation. For a symmetric requirement, only bipartitions need be checked, equivalently every proper subset must have cut degree at least twice its requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[h\text{ non-increasing}\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[(15.44)\text{ alone is sufficient}\bigr],\qquad \bigl[h\text{ symmetric}\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[(15.44)\text{ for }|\mathcal P|=2\iff d_G(X)\ge2h(X)\ \forall X\subset V\text{ is sufficient}\bigr]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of pairwise weighted connectivity by the prefix of an MA-ordering forest decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $k\ge 1$, let $F_1,\ldots,F_k$ be the first $k$ forests in a forest decomposition of a graph $G=(V,E)$ belonging to an MA ordering, and set $G_k=(V,F_1\cup\cdots\cup F_k)$. Suppose that, for every pair of vertices $u,v$, the number of parallel $uv$-edges is at most $\min\{g(u),g(v)\}$. If $\lambda_g(x,y;G)\ge k$ for every pair of vertices $x,y$, then $\lambda_g(x,y;G_k)\ge k$ for every pair of vertices $x,y$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a graph has pairwise g-connectivity at least k and its parallel-edge multiplicities obey the stated g-bounds, then the subgraph formed by the first k forests of an MA-ordering forest decomposition still has pairwise g-connectivity at least k.
assumptions_latex: G_k=(V,F_1\cup\cdots\cup F_k),\text{ where }F_1,\ldots,F_k\text{ are the first }k\text{ forests of an MA-ordering forest decomposition of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_g(x,y;G_k)\ge k\quad\forall x,y\in V

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed \(k\)-cut certificate of \(D\) is a spanning subdigraph \(H=(V,B)\) such that \[\min\{k,|\varrho_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\varrho_D(S)|\}\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\] Directed sparse-certificate constructions produce such an \(H\) with \(O(k|V|)\) arcs. Therefore every in-cut having fewer than \(k\) arcs is retained exactly, and every larger in-cut retains at least \(k\) arcs. Applying the same statement to the reversal of \(D\) yields an out-cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed k-certificate has O(kn) arcs and preserves small in-cuts exactly; arc reversal provides the corresponding out-cut guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deletable Entering Edge in Rooted Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\varrho_D(v)\) denotes the indegree of \(v\), and rooted \(k\)-edge-connectivity to \(T\) means that every terminal is reachable from the root by at least \(k\) edge-disjoint directed paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(r_0\in V\), and let \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{r_0\}\). Suppose \(D\) is \(k\)-edge-connected from \(r_0\) to every vertex of \(T\). If \(\varrho_D(t)>k\) for some \(t\in T\), then some edge entering \(t\) can be deleted while preserving this rooted \(k\)-edge-connectivity. Consequently, if \(D\) is edge-deletion-minimal and rooted \(k\)-edge-connected to every nonroot vertex, then \(\varrho_D(r_0)=0\) and \(\varrho_D(v)=k\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{r_0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a terminal in a root-to-terminal k-edge-connected digraph has indegree greater than k, an entering edge can be deleted without destroying the required connectivity. Hence every nonroot vertex of an edge-minimal rooted k-edge-connected digraph has indegree exactly k, while the root has indegree zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists e\in\delta_D^-(t)\;\forall x\in T:\ \lambda(r_0,x;D-e)\ge k;\quad\text{and under edge-minimality, }\varrho_D(r_0)=0,\ \varrho_D(v)=k\ \forall v\ne r_0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition assumes a digraph, a distinguished root, and a bound function \(g\) for which the rooted connectivity values \(\lambda_g\) are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) with root \(r_0\) is rooted \(\lambda_g\)-minimal if, for every edge \(e\in A\), there exists a vertex \(v\in V\setminus\{r_0\}\) such that \(\lambda_g(r_0,v;D-e)<\lambda_g(r_0,v;D)\). When \(g\equiv\infty\), this is called rooted \(\lambda\)-minimality; when \(g\equiv1\), it is called rooted \(\kappa\)-minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted digraph is λ_g-minimal when deleting any edge strictly reduces the rooted g-bounded connectivity to at least one nonroot vertex. The cases g identically infinity and g identically one are called rooted λ-minimality and rooted κ-minimality, respectively.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral capacities, Ford-Fulkerson performs at most \(F^*\) augmentations. If each residual-path search takes \(O(|E|)\) time, including the final unsuccessful search, its running time is \(O(|E|(F^*+1))\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral Ford-Fulkerson uses at most F* augmentations and O(m(F*+1)) time, which is polynomial in capacity magnitudes but can be exponential in their binary encoding length.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-encoding complexity for maximum-flow algorithms with rational capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed maximum-flow instance with \(n\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, and binary-encoded rational capacities of total encoding length \(L\), an algorithm is weakly polynomial if its running time is bounded by \(p(n,m,L)\) for some polynomial \(p\). Equivalently, the bound may depend polynomially on the bit lengths of the numerical data and intermediate quantities. Thus a dependence polynomial in \(\log U\), where \(U\) bounds integral capacities, is permitted, while dependence polynomial in \(U\) itself is not.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Flow Witness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-flow component of a paired flow–cut optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have capacities \(u:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) and distinct terminals \(s,t\). A maximum-flow witness candidate is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) whose certificate checks are \(0\le f_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\), and flow conservation \(\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\). Its reported value is \(|f|=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(s)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(s)}f_a\). Optimality follows when a paired cut witness has capacity \(|f|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The witness supplies a capacity-feasible, conserving flow and its value; equality with a cut capacity certifies maximality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of reported value }|f|

notation.meaning: Arcs leaving and entering vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut Witness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut component of a paired flow–cut optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed capacitated graph \(G=(V,A)\) with terminals \(s,t\), a minimum-cut witness candidate is a set \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\). Its verifiable reported capacity is \(c(S)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a\), where \(\delta^+(S)=\{(x,y)\in A:x\in S,\ y\notin S\}\). The set and this sum certify a valid upper bound on every feasible flow value; minimality follows when a paired feasible flow has value \(c(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The witness supplies an s–t vertex separation and its outgoing capacity; matching that capacity with a feasible flow proves minimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |f|\le c(S)\text{ for every feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow }f

notation.meaning: Arcs leaving the vertex set S

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Cut Value Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality check completing a paired maximum-flow/minimum-cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) pass the feasible-flow checks and let \(S\) pass the \(s\)-\(t\) cut checks. If the independently computed quantities satisfy \(|f|=c(S)\), then weak flow–cut duality gives \(|f|\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{flow}}\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{cut}}\le c(S)\). Hence every inequality is equality: \(f\) is a maximum flow, \(S\) is a minimum cut, and their common value is the optimum. This equality is directly checkable by summing the listed arc values and capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and valid cut with equal values jointly certify that the flow is maximum and the cut is minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |f|=c(S)\Longrightarrow |f|=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{flow}}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{cut}}=c(S)

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation-Feasibility Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct primal certificate for circulation with lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) and bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\), a circulation-feasibility output is a vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\). It is accepted exactly when \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) and \(\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a\) for every \(v\in V\). These finitely many bound and conservation checks directly certify that the bounded-circulation instance is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible output is an arc vector satisfying every lower bound, upper bound, and vertex conservation equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:\ell\le y\le u,\ By=0\}

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation-Infeasibility Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman-type violating-set certificate for bounded-circulation infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\) on a finite directed graph, an infeasibility output is a set \(X\subseteq V\) satisfying \(\sum_{a\in\delta^-(X)}\ell_a>\sum_{a\in\delta^+(X)}u_a\). Any conserving circulation would have equal total flow entering and leaving \(X\), while its entering flow is at least the left side and its leaving flow is at most the right side. Therefore the displayed strict inequality is a finite, directly checkable certificate that no circulation respecting all bounds exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set whose mandatory inflow exceeds its possible outflow certifies that the bounded-circulation instance is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{a\in\delta^-(X)}\ell_a>\sum_{a\in\delta^+(X)}u_a\Longrightarrow\nexists x:\ell\le x\le u,\ Bx=0

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Global-Cut Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gomory–Hu tree representation for all-pairs cuts in an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with nonnegative capacities. A compact global-cut output is a weighted tree \(T\) on vertex set \(V\) such that, for every distinct \(s,t\in V\), the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut value in \(G\) equals the minimum edge weight on the unique \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(T\). Moreover, deleting an edge of minimum weight on that path yields a bipartition inducing a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\). The output uses only \(|V|-1\) weighted edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted Gomory–Hu tree stores every pairwise minimum-cut value and a corresponding cut using only n−1 tree edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Arc Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired-arc representation of residual capacities for directed maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each original arc \(a=(v,w)\) with capacity \(u_a\) and current flow \(f_a\), residual-arc storage maintains a forward record \(a\) with residual capacity \(r_a=u_a-f_a\) and a reverse record \(a^{\mathrm{rev}}=(w,v)\) with residual capacity \(r_{a^{\mathrm{rev}}}=f_a\). The two records contain mutual reverse indices, so augmenting by \(\Delta\le r_a\) updates them in constant time as \(r_a\leftarrow r_a-\Delta\) and \(r_{a^{\mathrm{rev}}}\leftarrow r_{a^{\mathrm{rev}}}+\Delta\). Only records with positive residual capacity are traversable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each arc is stored with a linked reverse arc, permitting constant-time residual updates after an augmentation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_a=u_a-f_a,\quad r_{a^{\mathrm{rev}}}=f_a

children.title: FIFO Queue Scheduling
children.top_down_role: First-in-first-out processing interfaces for active objects.

knowledge_statements.title: FIFO Queue Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-vertex scheduling rule for a generic push–relabel maximum-flow algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a valid push–relabel preflow, place every active vertex other than \(s,t\) into a queue, and mark it present. Repeatedly remove the front vertex \(v\), discharge it by admissible pushes and relabels until either its excess becomes zero or the implementation's discharge ends, and append each newly active unmarked vertex to the rear. If \(v\) remains active after discharge, append it to the rear. Stop when the queue is empty; the resulting preflow is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow under the standard valid-label push–relabel invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FIFO scheduling processes active vertices in first-in, first-out order, appending newly active or still-active vertices to the queue rear.
assumptions_latex: \text{push and relabel operations preserve valid-label preflow invariants}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\Longrightarrow e(v)=0\quad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\})

knowledge_statements.title: LIFO Stack Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-vertex stack scheduling for a generic push–relabel maximum-flow algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a valid push–relabel preflow and push every active vertex other than \(s,t\) onto a stack, recording membership to avoid duplicates. Repeatedly pop the top vertex \(v\), discharge it using admissible pushes and relabels, and immediately push any newly active unstacked vertex. If \(v\) remains active when its discharge ends, push \(v\) again. Stop when the stack is empty; then no internal vertex has positive excess, and the standard push–relabel invariants imply that the resulting preflow is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LIFO scheduling always processes the most recently stacked active vertex and restacks any vertex that remains active.
assumptions_latex: \text{push and relabel operations preserve valid-label preflow invariants}

knowledge_statements.title: Bucketed Priority Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Highest-label bucket scheduling for push–relabel maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a valid push–relabel preflow and maintain buckets \(B_k\) containing active internal vertices of integer label \(k\). Repeatedly choose a vertex \(v\) from the nonempty bucket of largest index, discharge it by admissible pushes and relabels, move every newly active vertex to the bucket matching its current label, and move \(v\) whenever relabeling changes its label. Remove vertices whose excess becomes zero. Stop when all buckets are empty; the resulting preflow is a maximum flow under the standard valid-label push–relabel invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Highest-label bucket scheduling groups active vertices by label and repeatedly discharges one from the greatest nonempty label bucket.

children.title: Schedule-Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Performance differences attributable to the selected scheduling discipline.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), nonnegative integral capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), and an integral feasible initial flow \(f_0\).
Each scheduled path is an \(s\)-\(t\) path of positive residual capacity and is augmented by its bottleneck residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every such schedule terminates after at most \(F^*-|f_0|\) augmentations under integral capacities, whereas arbitrary nonnegative real capacities admit schedule-dependent nontermination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of generic augmenting-path behavior on the eligible-path scheduling rule.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Primal-Dual Algorithms for Max-Flow and Shortest Path: Ford-Fulkerson and Dijkstra p. 117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a schedule select an augmenting path in each residual network of an integral feasible flow. Every residual capacity is then integral, so each augmentation increases the flow value by at least one. Consequently, every schedule terminates after at most \(F^*-|f_0|\) augmentations. With arbitrary nonnegative real capacities, admissibility alone does not ensure termination. Scheduling may therefore preserve the conditional correctness statement that termination with no augmenting path implies maximality while changing termination and complexity guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integral capacities and an integral initial feasible flow, every augmenting schedule terminates after at most the difference between the maximum and initial flow values, although its running time can vary. With real capacities, an admissible schedule may fail to terminate.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Tree Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract forest interface used to aggregate and update residual information along paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dynamic-tree interface maintains a forest on a vertex set \(V\), with a real label on every forest edge. It supports \(\operatorname{link}(v,w,a)\), joining roots in distinct trees by an edge of label \(a\); \(\operatorname{cut}(v,w)\), deleting a forest edge; \(\operatorname{pathmin}(v,w)\), returning a minimum-label edge on the unique forest path; and \(\operatorname{pathadd}(v,w,\delta)\), adding \(\delta\) to every label on that path. A valid implementation must preserve the forest invariant and return exactly the aggregates defined by the current represented forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic-tree interface maintains a changing forest and supports link, cut, path-minimum, and path-update operations used to batch residual-flow work.
assumptions_latex: The represented graph is always a forest, so every connected vertex pair has a unique forest path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each operation has the stated effect on the represented forest and its edge labels.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Dynamic-Tree Interfaces container and is mathematically coherent, but it has no citation. A specific authoritative locator for the dynamic-tree operations and invariants is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Initial Feasible Flow Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-start augmentation from a flow feasible for the modified instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a modified network \((G,u',s,t)\) and a previously computed flow \(f\) satisfying conservation and \(0\le f_e\le u'_e\) for every arc. Initialize the residual network using forward capacity \(u'_e-f_e\) and reverse capacity \(f_e\). Repeatedly augment along any residual \(s\)-\(t\) path until none exists, and output the resulting flow \(f'\). The output is a maximum flow for the modified capacities; no zero-flow restart is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the old flow remains feasible after modification, initialize the new residual network from it and continue augmenting to a new maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(f\) is feasible under the modified capacities \(u'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned flow \(f'\) is maximum for \((G,u',s,t)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree-basis augmentation and cut optimality test for maximum flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to a connected source-destination network whose arc capacities are equal in both directions; includes degenerate zero-augmentation handling and the terminal cut test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a connected network have source $A$, destination $B$, and equal capacities in both directions on every arc. Maintain two arc-disjoint subtrees $T_A$ and $T_B$, rooted at $A$ and $B$, such that every intermediate node belongs to exactly one tree. Introduce an unmarked arc from $T_A$ to $T_B$, augment by the largest feasible amount along the resulting unique $A$-$B$ chain—decreasing existing flow on chain arcs traversed oppositely—and mark a saturated limiting arc. If the augmentation is zero because an unmarked chain arc is already at its bound, mark that blocking arc and update the trees. Repeat while an admissible connecting arc or a marked cut arc carrying flow from $T_B$ toward $T_A$ permits another chain augmentation. When no unmarked arc joins $T_A$ to $T_B$ and every marked arc crossing the induced cut carries flow from $T_A$ to $T_B$, the current feasible flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a connected network with equal capacity in both directions, maintain one tree rooted at the source and another rooted at the destination, partitioning the intermediate nodes. Add an unmarked arc between the trees and augment as much as possible along the unique source-to-destination chain, reducing flow on arcs used backward and marking a limiting saturated arc. In a degenerate zero-increase step, mark the already saturated blocking arc. Continue whenever another connecting chain can increase flow, including through a marked cut arc whose current flow points toward the source side. If no unmarked arc crosses the two-tree cut and every marked crossing arc carries flow from the source tree to the destination tree, the feasible flow is optimal.

u_{ij}=u_{ji}\text{ for each bidirectional arc pair}.
T_A\text{ and }T_B\text{ are rooted subtrees such that each intermediate node belongs to exactly one of them}.
x\text{ satisfies capacity bounds and flow conservation before each augmentation}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iterations preserve feasibility, and the stated terminal cut condition certifies that }x\text{ is a maximum }A\text{-}B\text{ flow}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ford–Fulkerson labeling method initialized by any feasible integer flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from a feasible integer flow $x$, form a residual network containing $(i,j)$ with residual capacity $u_{ij}-x_{ij}$ whenever $x_{ij}<u_{ij}$ and $(j,i)$ with residual capacity $x_{ij}$ whenever $x_{ij}>0$. While a source–sink residual path $P$ exists, augment by $\Delta=\min_{a\in P}\Delta_a$, increasing original forward-arc flows and decreasing original reverse-arc flows. With finite integer capacities, the process terminates. If no residual source–sink path exists and $X$ is the set reachable from the source, then every forward cut arc is saturated, every reverse cut arc has zero flow, and $f=u[X,\bar X]$; hence the current flow is maximum and the cut is minimum.

Finite integer capacities ensure termination. knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Capacity Nontermination Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ford–Fulkerson with arbitrary augmenting paths over real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Ford–Fulkerson on a finite network, integrality of capacities guarantees finite termination because every augmentation increases the flow value by at least one. This guarantee does not extend to arbitrary nonnegative real capacities: there exist finite networks with irrational capacities and admissible choices of augmenting paths for which the augmentation values form an infinite sequence, the algorithm never reaches a flow with no augmenting path, and the limiting flow value can be strictly smaller than the maximum-flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ford–Fulkerson always terminates for integral capacities, but irrational capacities admit path schedules with infinitely many augmentations and even a suboptimal limiting value.
assumptions_latex: Ford–Fulkerson always augments by the bottleneck residual capacity of the selected path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite termination for arbitrary path selection fails when capacities may be irrational.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose integral capacities are encoded in binary and \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\). The capacity fields use \(O(m\log(U+1))\) bits. Starting from the zero flow, arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson performs at most \(F^*\le mU\) augmentations, so an \(O(m)\)-time augmentation implementation has running time \(O(m^2U)\). Because \(U\) can be exponential in its binary encoding length, this is pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in the input length. If capacities are encoded in unary or are polynomially bounded in \(n+m\), the same capacity-dependent bound is polynomial in the encoded input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With binary capacities, the numerical value of the largest capacity can be exponential in its encoding length, so the capacity-dependent Ford–Fulkerson bound is pseudopolynomial. The same bound is polynomial for unary-encoded or polynomially bounded capacities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have lower bounds \(\ell_e\) and upper bounds \(u_e\) satisfying \(\ell_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\). knowledge_statements.title: Nonnetwork Side Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows how an added linear side constraint can destroy network-flow integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two parallel arcs from \(s\) to \(t\), with variables \(x_1,x_2\), unit capacities, and one unit of supply at \(s\). The network constraints are \(x_1+x_2=1\) and \(0\le x_i\le1\), whose extreme points are integral. Adding the nonnetwork side constraint \(x_1=x_2\) leaves the unique feasible point \(x_1=x_2=\tfrac12\). Thus an arbitrary side constraint need not preserve the integrality or pure circulation structure of a network-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupling equality can reduce an integral network-flow polytope to a single fractional feasible point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a fixed-terminal minimum cut from a global minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed versus Undirected Cut Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies complement symmetry as an undirected property that directed cuts lack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected capacitated graph, every proper set \(S\subset V\) satisfies \(c(\delta(S))=c(\delta(V\setminus S))\). In a directed graph the relevant outgoing capacities can differ: with arcs \(u\to v\) and \(v\to u\) of capacities \(1\) and \(2\), one has \(c(\delta^+(\{u\}))=1\) but \(c(\delta^+(\{v\}))=2\). Consequently, undirected arguments relying on complementary-cut symmetry do not transfer directly to directed cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Undirected cuts are symmetric under complementation, while directed outgoing cuts can have different capacities in opposite directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(\delta(S))=c(\delta(V\setminus S))\) is not generally valid with \(\delta\) replaced by \(\delta^+\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gomory-Hu Tree Domain Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits symmetric Gomory–Hu tree representations to undirected all-pairs cut values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted Gomory–Hu tree represents an undirected graph when, for every distinct \(s,t\), the graph value \(\lambda(s,t)\) equals the minimum edge weight on the unique tree path from \(s\) to \(t\). This tree value is symmetric. A directed graph with capacities \(c(u,v)=1\) and \(c(v,u)=2\) has \(\lambda(u,v)=1\) and \(\lambda(v,u)=2\); therefore no undirected weighted tree can represent all its ordered-pair minimum-cut values in this manner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree bottleneck values are symmetric, so one Gomory–Hu tree cannot encode asymmetric directed minimum-cut values.
assumptions_latex: Directed minimum cuts use outgoing cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(u,v)\ne\lambda(v,u)\) precludes a single undirected Gomory–Hu tree representation.

notation.meaning: minimum directed or undirected s-t cut value, as specified

knowledge_statements.title: Cactus Representation Domain Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricts the classical cactus encoding to global minimum cuts of undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected capacitated graph, a minimum-cut cactus encodes the bipartitions attaining the global minimum-cut value: deleting a cactus bridge, or two edges from one cactus cycle, induces such a bipartition through the vertex map. This representation concerns the family of global minimum cuts. It does not, without additional hypotheses or a different construction, encode every minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut for every pair, arbitrary nonminimum cuts, or asymmetric directed-cut values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical cut cactus encodes undirected global minimum cuts, not arbitrary cuts or general directed cut families.
assumptions_latex: The represented graph is finite, undirected, and has nonnegative capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cactus domain is \(\{S: c(\delta(S))=\lambda_{m global}\}\), modulo complementary shores.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates cost optimization from the capacity-only max-flow/min-cut equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two parallel arcs from \(s\) to \(t\) each have capacity \(1\), with costs \(0\) and \(1\), and require one unit of flow. Both arcs support the same feasible flow value and cross exactly the same source-sink cuts, but the unique minimum-cost solution uses the zero-cost arc. Thus cut capacity alone determines neither the minimum cost nor the optimizing flow; minimum-cost flow requires objective-cost information beyond classical max-flow/min-cut data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the capacitated, fixed-throughput minimum-cost flow problem on a directed network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), arc capacities \(b\), nonnegative arc costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}_+\), and prescribed value \(v_0\in\mathbb{R}_+\). If \(A\) is the node-arc incidence matrix and \(d_s=-1\), \(d_t=1\), and \(d_i=0\) otherwise, the fixed-value minimum-cost flow problem is
\[
\min_{f}\;c^{\mathsf T}f\quad\text{subject to}\quad Af=-v_0d,\qquad 0\le f\le b.
\]
Thus it selects, among all feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flows of value \(v_0\), one having minimum total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a capacitated directed network with nonnegative arc costs and a prescribed nonnegative flow value, find a feasible source-to-sink flow of that value having minimum total arc cost. Equivalently, minimize cᵀf subject to flow conservation with the prescribed source and sink imbalance and the arc bounds 0 ≤ f ≤ b.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a directed graph with source }s\text{ and sink }t.
A\text{ is the node-arc incidence matrix}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. For commodities \(k\) with terminal pairs \((s_k,t_k)\), demands \(d_k\ge 0\), and shared edge capacities \(u_e\ge 0\), feasibility implies every cut inequality \(\sum_{k:\,|\{s_k,t_k\}\cap S|=1} d_k\le \sum_{e\in\delta(S)}u_e\) for \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). Hence the single-commodity equivalence between feasible throughput and a minimum-cut value does not transfer unchanged.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). knowledge_statements.title: Gain Network Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the all-amplifying regime of a generalized flow network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized flow network is in the gain regime when every arc \(e=(i,j)\) has multiplier \(\gamma_e\ge1\), and sending \(x_e\ge0\) units from \(i\) makes \(\gamma_e x_e\) units available at \(j\). For each transshipment vertex \(v\), generalized conservation compares received and dispatched amounts through \(\sum_{e=(i,v)}\gamma_e x_e-\sum_{e=(v,j)}x_e=b_v\). The classical flow regime is the special case \(\gamma_e=1\) for all arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a gain network, every arc preserves or amplifies flow according to a multiplier at least one.
assumptions_latex: The network is directed and finite.
Arc flows and multipliers are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The gain regime is characterized by \(\gamma_e\ge1\) for every arc \(e\).

notation.meaning: prescribed generalized net inflow at v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Flow-Dominating Minimum-Capacity Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies a greatest pairwise flow function among minimum-capacity feasible syntheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the pairwise network-synthesis problem, let $u(x)$ denote the node requirement level used by the capacity lower bound and define $\bar r(x,y)=\min\{u(x),u(y)\}$. Synthesis with requirements $\bar r$ yields a feasible minimum-capacity network $\bar G$ satisfying $\bar v(x,y)=\bar r(x,y)$ for every pair. Moreover, for every other feasible minimum-capacity network with flow function $v$, $\bar v(x,y)\ge v(x,y)$ for all $x,y$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized gain–loss flow and minimum-loss objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines arc transformation, capacity and node-balance constraints, flow loss, and the two fixed-terminal-value optimization forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc $(i,j)$, let $m_{ij}\ge 0$ and let $x_{ij}$ denote the flow entering the arc, so that $m_{ij}x_{ij}$ leaves its head. Require $0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}$ and, for every node $i$, \[\sum_j m_{ji}x_{ji}-\sum_j x_{ij}=\begin{cases}-v_s,&i=s,\\0,&i\notin\{s,t\},\\v_t,&i=t.\end{cases}\] An arc is lossy when $0<m_{ij}<1$, gainy when $m_{ij}>1$, and conventional when $m_{ij}=1$. The flow loss is $v_s-v_t$; minimum loss means maximizing $v_t$ for prescribed $v_s$, or minimizing $v_s$ for prescribed $v_t$. In general $v_s$ need not equal $v_t$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc multiplies its entering flow by a nonnegative factor before delivery at its head. Feasible flows obey arc capacities and transformed node balances. Loss is the source value minus the sink value, and minimizing it means maximizing the sink value at a fixed source value or minimizing the source value at a fixed sink value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{loss}(x)=v_s-v_t,\qquad \min\operatorname{loss}\equiv\max v_t\text{ for fixed }v_s\equiv\min v_s\text{ for fixed }v_t.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Gain-Loss Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies generalized-flow cycles by their multiplicative gain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed cycle \(C=(e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) in a generalized network, define \(\Gamma(C)=\prod_{r=1}^m\gamma_{e_r}\). One traversal maps an entering amount \(z\) to \(\Gamma(C)z\), provided the corresponding arc flows respect capacities. The cycle is amplifying when \(\Gamma(C)>1\), balanced when \(\Gamma(C)=1\), and dissipative when \(\Gamma(C)<1\). Thus a cycle containing both gain and loss arcs is classified by their product, not by either arc type alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The product of arc multipliers determines whether a mixed gain-loss cycle amplifies, preserves, or dissipates flow.
assumptions_latex: All cycle multipliers are strictly positive.
Arc capacities permit the stated traversal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma(C)>1\), \(=1\), or \(<1\) determines amplification, balance, or dissipation, respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Flow-Cut Transfer Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits failure of raw-capacity cut equality in a generalized gain network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the path \(s\to v\to t\). Give the first arc capacity \(1\) and gain \(2\), and the second arc capacity \(2\) and gain \(1\). Dispatching one unit from \(s\) delivers two units to \(v\) and then to \(t\), so the maximum delivered value is \(2\). Yet the ordinary capacity of the cut \(\{s\}\) is \(1\). Therefore the classical equality between delivered flow and the minimum raw-capacity cut fails when gains differ from one.

knowledge_statements.title: Temporal Flow Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a discrete-time flow with capacities and arc transit times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete-time temporal flow on horizon \(T\in\mathbb N\) assigns \(x_{e,\theta}\ge0\) to each arc \(e=(v,w)\) and departure time \(\theta\) with \(\theta+\tau_e\le T\), subject to \(x_{e,\theta}\le u_{e,\theta}\). Flow dispatched at time \(\theta\) reaches \(w\) at time \(\theta+\tau_e\). At each nonterminal vertex and time, cumulative departures cannot exceed cumulative arrivals plus initial inventory; equality is imposed when waiting or storage is disallowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal flow specifies departure-time quantities whose capacity use and downstream arrival are indexed by time and transit delay.
assumptions_latex: Time is discrete with finite horizon \(T\).
Waiting is allowed unless explicitly prohibited.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(x_{e,\theta}\) consumes capacity at departure time \(\theta\) and arrives at time \(\theta+\tau_e\).

children.title: Time-Dependent Network Data

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Network Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic continuous-time data on a finite directed network and finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) and a horizon \(T>0\). Time-dependent network data consist of measurable functions \(u_a:[0,T]\to[0,\infty]\) and \(\tau_a:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)\) for every arc \(a\in A\), together with measurable node supplies \(b_v:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}\) for every \(v\in V\). Here \(u_a(t)\) bounds the rate entering arc \(a\) at departure time \(t\), \(\tau_a(t)\) is its transit time, and \(b_v(t)>0\) denotes external injection at node \(v\). Data are horizon-compatible when \(t+\tau_a(t)\le T\) for every permitted departure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temporal network data assign each arc a capacity and transit time depending on departure time, and each node a time-dependent external supply, over a fixed horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple \(\bigl(G,T,(u_a,\tau_a)_{a\in A},(b_v)_{v\in V}\bigr)\) defines deterministic continuous-time network data.

children.title: Transit-Time Constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Transit-Time Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage-free continuous-time conservation with constant arc transit times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_a:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)\) be the departure-rate function on arc \(a\), extended by \(x_a(t)=0\) outside \([0,T]\). For fixed transit times \(\tau_a\ge 0\), flow dispatched on \(a=(v,w)\) at time \(t\) reaches \(w\) at time \(t+\tau_a\). A storage-free temporal flow satisfies, for almost every \(t\in[0,T]\) and every node \(v\), \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a(t)-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a(t-\tau_a)=b_v(t),\qquad 0\le x_a(t)\le u_a(t).\] Thus incoming flow is available only after its arc transit delay.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Departing flow reaches an arc’s head only after the prescribed delay; conservation therefore compares current departures with appropriately delayed incoming rates.
assumptions_latex: Waiting or storage at intermediate nodes is excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires the delayed conservation equations and the pointwise capacity bounds to hold almost everywhere on \([0,T]\).

children.title: Static Reduction Limits
children.top_down_role: Boundaries on representing temporal or dynamically changing flow problems as ordinary static instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Static Reduction Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary for finite, interval-based time-expanded networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a temporal network having one arc \(a\), horizon \([0,1]\), zero transit time, and departure capacity \(u_a(t)=t\). Any finite-layer static expansion whose temporal arc copies represent constant rates on finitely many time intervals induces a step-function upper bound \(\widehat u_a\). Exact preservation of all feasible departure-rate functions would require \(\widehat u_a(t)=u_a(t)\) almost everywhere, which is impossible because no finite step function equals \(t\) almost everywhere on \([0,1]\). Hence finite interval-based time expansion is not an exact static reduction for arbitrary continuous time-dependent data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite time expansions exactly represent only suitably discretized data; even the capacity function u(t)=t cannot be preserved by finitely many constant-rate layers.
assumptions_latex: Time layers form a finite partition of \([0,1]\).
Each temporal arc copy has a constant rate bound on its interval.
Reduction exactness means preserving every feasible departure-rate function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite interval-based static expansion exactly represents the temporal capacity \(u_a(t)=t\) under pointwise rate feasibility.

notation.meaning: capacity induced by the finite static expansion

review_flags: The counterexample is mathematically direct, but the intended class of static reductions must be checked against an authoritative temporal-flow source.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Algorithm Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination and encoding-length boundaries of arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run the Ford–Fulkerson method from the zero flow, choosing an arbitrary residual \(s\)-\(t\) path and augmenting by its residual bottleneck. If all capacities are nonnegative integers and the maximum-flow value is \(U\), every augmentation increases the flow value by at least one, so at most \(U\) augmentations occur. This bound is pseudopolynomial when capacities are binary encoded. For general irrational capacities, finite networks and legal augmenting-path choices exist for which the method performs infinitely many augmentations and never attains a maximum flow. Thus arbitrary-path augmentation is neither strongly polynomial nor unconditionally terminating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ford–Fulkerson terminates for integer capacities but has only a value-dependent bound; with irrational capacities, legal path choices can cause nontermination.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and nonnegative capacities.
Each iteration augments along an arbitrary residual \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integer capacities give at most \(U\) augmentations, whereas arbitrary irrational capacities do not guarantee termination.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite arc set and let an ordinary same-variable linear-cost representation assign the affine objective \(\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a+k\), where \(c_a\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(k\in\mathbb{R}\) are constants. Such a representation need not preserve a genuinely nonlinear separable objective \(\sum_{a\in A}C_a(x_a)\). In particular, for one arc with \(x_a\in[0,1]\) and \(C_a(x_a)=x_a^2\), there are no constants \(c_a,k\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(x_a^2=c_ax_a+k\) for every \(x_a\in[0,1]\). Thus this quadratic objective cannot be transferred exactly to an ordinary linear cost without changing the representation or the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordinary affine cost on unchanged continuous flow variables cannot exactly preserve every nonlinear convex objective; in particular, it cannot equal the one-arc quadratic cost on the whole interval from zero to one.
